chunks.t: A complete, type-safe CRUD abstraction for Drizzle ORM in NestJS: configure the connection once, extend one base class per entity, and inherit full CRUD.

nestjs-drizzle-crud is a thin abstraction over Drizzle ORM (https://orm.drizzle.team/) that gives every NestJS service a complete, type-safe CRUD surface by extending a single generic base class: find, findOne, findAll, create, update, delete, softDelete, restore, massCreate, massUpdate, massDelete and fullTextSearch, plus filtering, pagination, relations, hooks and transactions.

It works with both PostgreSQL and MySQL and handles the dialect differences (PostgreSQL's RETURNING vs MySQL's insertId) for you, so your service code is identical across databases.

The whole library is built on two steps:

Configure the database connection once. In your AppModule, call DrizzleCrudModule.forRoot(...) with the dialect, connection (either a connection string or a pre-built Drizzle instance), and the schema. The module creates and owns the connection, exposes it globally, and closes it on shutdown.

Per entity: extend the base, bind the table. For each entity, create an empty service class that extends SqlBaseCrudService, then register it in a feature module with DrizzleCrudModule.forFeature([{ service, table }]). The service gets every CRUD method automatically, fully typed against your entity.

That is the entire library surface. Everything else, including soft delete, bulk ops, full-text search, hooks, transactions and relations, is enabled through configuration rather than new APIs to learn.

Use nestjs-drizzle-crud when you want:

- A standard REST/JSON CRUD surface over a relational schema.
- To stop writing the same findAll / create / update boilerplate in every service.
- Type-safe query and result types inferred from your Drizzle schema.
- Soft delete, audit timestamps, and filtering/sorting out of the box.
- Bulk operations that roll back atomically when one row fails.
- A library that doesn't hide Drizzle. You can drop down to raw db.select() whenever you need to.

- Complex aggregate queries. If most of your endpoints are joins, window functions, or domain-specific reads, hand-written Drizzle will be clearer.
- Has-many / many-to-many relations. Only many-to-one / belongs-to relations are supported. Model those with custom service methods over this.config.db.
- Non-CRUD write patterns. If your writes are mostly multi-step domain operations (workflows, sagas), use a hand-rolled service and only pull in nestjs-drizzle-crud for the simple entities.
- GraphQL. The library returns plain objects shaped for REST. Use it with REST controllers; for GraphQL you'll write resolvers against the service methods directly.

That's it. Your UsersService already exposes find, findOne, findAll, create, update, delete, softDelete, restore, massCreate, massUpdate, count, exists, executeSqlTransaction, and fullTextSearch (Postgres), all typed against User.

Ready to wire it up? Head to the Quick start (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/quick-start) for a complete 5-minute walkthrough, or read Installation (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/installation) for the full peer-dependency matrix.

Add _count to rows with options.counts, one GROUP BY per relation and no N+1, and get grouped counts per column value with countBy(column, filters). Soft delete, scope and allowlists apply.

options.counts puts the number of related rows on each row under _count, with one grouped query per relation for the whole result. countBy(column, filters) returns how many rows have each value of a column. Both respect soft delete, the tenant scope and the allowlists.

c.s:
const page = await authors.findAll({}, {}, { counts: ['posts'] });
page.data[0]._count; // { posts: 10 }

chunks.t:
With one SELECT key, count( )... WHERE key IN (...) GROUP BY key per relation, for every row of the page at once, and the relations run concurrently. A page of 50 authors with counts: ['posts', 'tags'] is the data query, the count query and two grouped queries, never one per row. A has-many counts the related rows; a many-to-many counts the links whose target row is live.

counts works on find, findOne, findAll, findByCursor, and on the rows a write returns (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations-on-writes). When select narrows the columns, the key the count groups on is added back.

chunks.h: Can I count only some related rows?
chunks.t:
Pass an object instead of a list. Each value is a filter on the related table, or true for all of them:

The filter accepts everything a filter (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering) does, groups included.

- Only has-many and many-to-many relations. Counting a belongs-to, or a relation that is not configured, is a 400.
- Soft-deleted related rows are not counted.
- The relation must be allowed by loadableRelations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) when that list is set.
- Counts are top level: posts, not posts.comments.

From a query string,?counts=posts,tags sets options.counts. See Parse query strings (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing).

chunks.h: How do I count rows per column value?
chunks.t:
countBy(column, filters?, options?) returns one entry per value, largest group first, ties ordered by value:

It is one GROUP BY query. The column is a column of the table, or of a top-level belongs-to written as relation.column. Filters, options.search, the tenant scope (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy) and soft delete apply as they do in count, so soft-deleted rows are not counted unless you pass withDeleted. The column must be in filterableColumns (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) when that list is set, since grouping exposes its values the way filtering does. An unknown column is a 400. The type of value is a generic: countBy<string ('status').

- → Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations)
- → Relation filters: paths and some / none / every (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relation-filters)
- → Pagination: skip the count with withCount: false (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting#how-do-i-skip-the-count-query)

Set up nestjs-drizzle-crud rules for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI and other agents, and run the package MCP server.

The package ships two things for AI coding agents: a rules template you copy into your project so the agent follows the package conventions, and an MCP server that lets the agent read the package docs on demand. Both work with any agent, and neither adds a dependency.

chunks.h: Which file does my agent read?
chunks.t:
Copy the template to the filename your tool looks for:

Agent File in your project root 
--- --- 
OpenAI Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Zed, Cline, Windsurf, Jules AGENTS.md 
Claude Code CLAUDE.md 
Gemini CLI GEMINI.md 
Aider CONVENTIONS.md, then aider --read CONVENTIONS.md 

Each template is a pointer, not a copy. It contains one line:

AGENT.md ships inside the package and stays the single source of truth, so an upgrade updates the rules with it. If your agent does not resolve @ imports, paste the contents of AGENT.md in place of that line, or run the MCP server below so the agent can fetch the guidance itself.

Using several agents on one repo? Copy the template to each filename, or keep AGENTS.md and make the others a one-line pointer to it.

c.s:
cp node_modules/nestjs-drizzle-crud/AGENTS.template.md ./AGENTS.md      # most tools
cp node_modules/nestjs-drizzle-crud/CLAUDE.template.md ./CLAUDE.md      # Claude Code

chunks.h: What is in the rules file?
chunks.t: AGENT.md is written for an agent that is about to add an endpoint: that a service is normally an empty subclass, that the table goes in forFeature and not in the service, that filters are objects ({ age: { gte: 18 } }), that findAll returns { data, total, page, limit }, and which exception maps to which status code. It exists to stop the two most common mistakes, hand-writing repository code the base service already has, and injecting the database into a service.

The package includes an MCP server so an agent can search the docs while it works instead of guessing at the API:

It speaks JSON-RPC over stdio, has no dependencies, and serves the markdown that ships in the package. Register it once per project.

Tool Arguments Returns

search_docs query, optional limit The most relevant sections, best match first.

- Defining services (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/defining-services): what the agent is meant to produce.

Limit which columns a client may filter, sort, select and search, which relations it may load, and which columns create and update may write. Anything else is a 400.

Allowlists decide what a client may touch through a query or a request body. Set them per entity in forFeature; anything outside a set list is a 400, both in the service and in parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing).

Because a list endpoint that forwards the query string otherwise lets a client reach every column. Without selectableColumns,?fields=password_hash returns the hashes. Without filterableColumns,?password_hash[startsWith]=a lets a client guess one a character at a time. Without writableColumns, a body with role: 'admin' sets it, unless every DTO strips it. Set the lists on any entity a client can reach.

Key Checked on Entries 
--- --- --- 
filterableColumns findAll, findByCursor and count filters, groups included Columns, and relation.column for relation filters. 
sortableColumns a caller sortBy Columns, and relation.column for a belongs-to. The primary key is always allowed. 
selectableColumns options.select on every read Columns, and dotted paths at any depth (states.cities.name). The primary key is always allowed. 
searchableColumns options.search.columns and fullTextSearch Columns. parseQuery also uses it as the default search columns. 
loadableRelations options.relations and options.counts Relation paths. Listing states.cities allows states too. 
writableColumns create, update, upsert and the mass versions Columns. 
writableRelations nested create bodies, attach, detach, sync Relation names. Unset, nested writes are off and the link methods work on any many-to-many relation. See Relations on writes (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations-on-writes). 

filterableColumns also governs countBy (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates), and takes full dotted paths for deeper relation filters (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relation-filters) (state.country.code).
An unset list allows everything, which is how 3.3 behaved, except writableRelations, where unset means no nested writes. An empty list ([]) allows nothing.

findOne(where) is usually a server-side lookup (findOne({ email }) during login), so its where keys are not checked against filterableColumns; its select and relations are. The configured defaultSort is not checked either. For any other trusted call, pass skipAllowlists: true:

c.s: await users.count({ password_reset_token: token }, { skipAllowlists: true });

chunks.h: Which columns can a body write by default?
chunks.t:
Everything except the columns the package manages itself. Without writableColumns:

- the soft delete column is ignored on create and update,
- the primary key and the createdAt timestamp are ignored on update.

Ignored means dropped silently, so a PATCH body that echoes id back still works. An update that has nothing left to set is a 400.

With writableColumns set, any column outside the list is a 400 (Validation failed: the column "role" is not writable), the managed columns included. List the primary key there if your create path takes client supplied keys, such as uuids or natural keys. Keys that are not columns at all are ignored, as before.

1. Keep ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }) and real DTOs for request bodies.
2. Set writableColumns on every entity with a public create or update route.
3. Set selectableColumns and filterableColumns on every entity behind a list route, and leave secrets out of both.
4. Set loadableRelations when a related table holds data some callers must not see.

- → Parse query strings into filters (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing)
- → Column selection (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/column-selection)
- → Errors: what each 400 looks like (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/errors)

chunks.t:
Method Returns Notes 
--- --- --- 
find(id, options?) Promise By primary key. Skips soft-deleted rows. 
findOne(where, options?) Promise where is a Partial: exact, case-sensitive equality, null for IS NULL, or an operator object. undefined values are skipped; if nothing is left, or a key is not a column, it throws a 400 rather than returning an arbitrary row. 
findAll(filters?, pagination?, options?) Promise: { data, total, page, limit } withCount: false skips the count: total is null and hasMore is set (Pagination (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting#how-do-i-skip-the-count-query)). Supports options.search, and / or / not groups and multi-column or relation sortBy. An unknown filter key is a 400. Always ends ORDER BY with the primary key. See Filtering (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering) and Pagination (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting). 
findByCursor(filters?, pagination?, options?) Promise Keyset pagination: { data, limit, nextCursor, total? }. total only with count: true. See Cursor pagination (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/cursor-pagination). 
exists(id, options?) Promise<boolean Cheaper than find when you only need a yes/no. 
count(filters?, options?) Promise<number Total rows matching the filter and options.search, ignoring pagination. 
countBy(column, filters?, options?) Promise [{ value, count }] per value of a column or a belongs-to relation.column, largest first. One GROUP BY. See Aggregates (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates). 
parseId(raw) Promise<unknown Parses a route id by the primary key column: ParseIntPipe for an integer, ParseUUIDPipe for a uuid, BigInt for a bigint, the string otherwise. Bad input is a 400. 
idKind() 'int' \ 'bigint' \ 'uuid' \ 'string' What the primary key column holds. 
parseQuery(query, options?) ParsedCrudQuery Turns an HTTP query object into { filters, pagination, options,... } for this entity. See Parse query strings (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing).

Every read takes withDeleted / onlyDeleted to include or only return soft-deleted rows. See Soft delete (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete#how-do-i-list-soft-deleted-rows). Every read also takes counts for _count on each row (Aggregates (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates)), and on an entity with a scope (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy) every read only sees the caller's rows.

Method Returns Notes 
--- --- --- 
create(data, options?) Promise Runs validateCreate → mapCreateDtoToEntity → beforeCreate → insert → afterCreate. 
update(id, data, options?) Promise Throws EntityNotFoundException if missing, and ValidationFailedException (400) when data has no column to set. 
delete(id, options?) Promise<boolean Hard delete. 
softDelete(id, options?) Promise<boolean Sets deleted_at to now(). Requires soft delete enabled. 
restore(id, options?) Promise Clears deleted_at. Throws EntityNotFoundException if missing. 
forceDelete(id, options?) Promise<boolean Hard delete, soft-deleted or not. 
upsert(data, upsert?, options?) Promise ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (Postgres) or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (MySQL). upsert is { conflictTarget?, update? }. See Upsert (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/upsert). 
attach(id, relation, relatedIds, options?) Promise Links many-to-many rows through the join table; returns the row with the relation loaded. See Relations on writes (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations-on-writes). 
detach(id, relation, relatedIds?, options?) Promise Unlinks the ids, or every link when relatedIds is left out. 
sync(id, relation, relatedIds, options?) Promise Makes the links exactly relatedIds.

Writes take options.relations and options.counts and return the rows with them loaded. With versionColumn (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/optimistic-locking), update, softDelete, restore and delete take expectedVersion (or the version in the body) and answer a stale one with a 409. With global hooks (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events) on, every write raises a before and an after event.

create, update and upsert apply writableColumns (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists#which-columns-can-a-body-write-by-default). Without it, update ignores the primary key and createdAt, and both ignore the soft delete column.

chunks.h: Bulk (single transaction, rolls back on any failure)
chunks.t:
Method Returns 
--- --- 
massCreate(data[], options?) Promise 
massUpdate(ids[], data, options?) Promise 
massSoftDelete(ids[], options?) Promise<boolean 
massRestore(ids[], options?) Promise 
massDelete(ids[], options?) Promise<boolean 
massForceDelete(ids[], options?) Promise<boolean 
massUpsert(data[], upsert?, options?) Promise 

Each method is one statement for the whole set (plus one SELECT that checks the ids exist), and bulkMode: 'perItem' runs the single-row method per item instead. When the statement fails, the items that fail are named. Throws BulkOperationException on failure; its 400 body is { statusCode, error, message, errors: [{ index id, status, message }] }. See Bulk operations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/bulk-operations).

Method Returns Notes 
--- --- --- 
fullTextSearch(term, columns, pagination?, options?) Promise<{ data: T[]; total: number; page: number; limit: number } PostgreSQL only. Same envelope as findAll. to_tsvector(...) @@ plainto_tsquery(...) with ts_rank ordering, then the primary key. Always applies page and limit. An unknown column is a 400. Excludes soft-deleted rows when soft-delete is enabled.
executeSqlTransaction(callback) opens a transaction, runs the callback with the transaction handle, commits on success, rolls back on any throw.

relations eager-loads relations declared in the entity's config: a top-level belongs-to joins the main query, while has-many, many-to-many and every nested level add one batched query each for the whole result set. Never one query per row. See Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations).

select narrows the projection, and a dotted entry narrows an eager-loaded relation at any depth (['id', 'name', 'region.code', 'states.cities.name']). See Column selection (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/column-selection).

- → Errors: hTTP status code mapping for every exception (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/errors)
- → Config types, SqlCrudConfig and DrizzleCrudConfig (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/config-types)
- → Exports: the full public API surface (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/exports)

massCreate, massUpdate, massSoftDelete, massRestore, massDelete and massForceDelete: one statement for the whole set, in a transaction, with a 400 body that lists every failed item.

Bulk operations write the whole set with one statement, inside a single database transaction. If any item fails, the entire operation is rolled back and a BulkOperationException (400) is thrown. Its response body lists each failed item with its own status and message.

Method Returns Failure mode 
--- --- --- 
massCreate(data[], options?) Promise Tries every item, then throws BulkOperationException if any failed. 
massUpdate(ids[], data, options?) Promise Same. 
massSoftDelete(ids[], options?) Promise<boolean Same. 
massRestore(ids[], options?) Promise Same. 
massDelete(ids[], options?) Promise<boolean Same. 
massForceDelete(ids[], options?) Promise<boolean Same. Also deletes rows that are in the trash. 
massUpsert(data[], upsert, options?) Promise Same. See Upsert (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/upsert). 

Duplicate ids are written once. The rows come back in the order of the ids you passed.

chunks.h: How many queries does a bulk call cost?
chunks.t:
A fixed number, whatever the number of ids:

Method Statements 
--- --- 
massCreate one multi-row INSERT... RETURNING 
massUpdate one SELECT to check every id exists, one UPDATE... WHERE id IN (...) 
massSoftDelete, massRestore one SELECT, one UPDATE... WHERE id IN (...) 
massDelete, massForceDelete one SELECT, one DELETE... WHERE id IN (...) 
massUpsert one INSERT... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE 

So massUpdate over 100 ids is two queries, not two hundred. Without RETURNING (MySQL) one more SELECT reads the rows back. On MySQL, massCreate of rows with auto-increment keys inserts row by row, because MySQL only reports the first id of a multi-row insert.

All bulk methods wrap their work in a single transaction. If any row fails (constraint violation, FK error, validation, etc.), the transaction is rolled back. No partial writes are visible to subsequent reads.

When the set statement fails, the package needs to know which items caused it. It replays the batch one item at a time, each in its own savepoint, all inside an outer savepoint that is rolled back at the end, and reports the items that fail. That replay only runs on the failure path, and it leaves nothing behind even inside your own transaction. Two rows of the same batch that clash only with each other show up as the second of the pair, because the replay has already written the first. When no single item fails, the statement's own error is thrown instead.

A bulk operation that succeeds returns its full result. A bulk operation
that fails throws BulkOperationException and none of the rows are
modified. Use this as a guarantee, not just an optimization.

chunks.h: Can I still run one query per item?
chunks.t: Yes, with bulkMode: 'perItem'. Each item then goes through the single-row method (create, update, delete,...) in its own savepoint, as in 3.3. Use it when a per-item hook must see the rows written before it.

c.s: await service.massUpdate(ids, { status: 'archived' }, { bulkMode: 'perItem' });

chunks.h: What does a failed bulk call return over HTTP?
chunks.t:
A 400 whose body names every failed item. massCreate identifies an item by its index in the input array; the other methods use the id you passed:

status and message are what that item alone would have produced: 409 for a duplicate, 404 for a missing id, 400 for bad input. An error that is not an HTTP exception (a driver fault, say) appears as status: 500 with the message Internal server error, so SQL and parameters never reach the client. Let the exception propagate and Nest's default filter sends this body as is.
The errors property keeps the original Error objects for logging. The response body carries the safe summary.

The standard beforeCreate / afterCreate (and the corresponding update / delete / softDelete / restore hooks) fire once per row, in array order. A massCreate([a, b, c]) calls validateCreate and beforeCreate three times, then runs the one insert, then calls afterCreate three times. massUpdate checks the ids first, then calls validateUpdate and beforeUpdate once per id.

Module-level events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events) fire once for the whole call instead, with bulk: true and every id, before and after the statement and inside the transaction.

If any row's hook throws, that item is recorded as failed, the rest still run, and nothing is written. If beforeUpdate returns different data for different ids, one SET cannot express it, so massUpdate writes those rows with one UPDATE each.

All bulk methods accept the same SqlOperationOptions as their non-bulk counterparts. In particular, you can pass a custom transaction:

See Transactions (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/transactions) for the full pattern.

relations and counts load onto the rows a bulk write returns with one query per relation (Relations on writes (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations-on-writes)). On a scoped entity (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy) an id of another tenant is a 404 entry and nothing is written. With optimistic locking (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/optimistic-locking), every written row's version goes up by one, and expectedVersions: { '1': 4 } turns an id at another version into a 409 entry.

Bulk methods don't paginate. They accept the full array in memory and execute it as a single transaction. For very large bulk operations (thousands of rows), consider:

- Chunking on the caller side. Process arrays in batches of 100–500 rows and call massCreate per batch.
- Switching to a streaming insert. Write a custom method that uses Drizzle's db.insert(...).values(chunk).execute() chain with explicit chunking.

The cap is on the database side, not the package. Single transactions holding thousands of row locks can starve other connections.

- → Transactions, executeSqlTransaction for cross-service atomicity (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/transactions)
- → Errors, BulkOperationException → 400 mapping and per-row error details (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/errors)
- → Hooks & validation: per-row hooks during bulk ops (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/hooks-validation)

Release-by-release behavior changes for nestjs-drizzle-crud. Mirrors CHANGELOG.md shipped in the npm tarball.

This page mirrors the CHANGELOG.md (https://www.npmjs.com/package/nestjs-drizzle-crud?activeTab=code) shipped in the npm tarball. Feature pages describe current behavior; this page is the historical record. If something here disagrees with a feature page, the feature page wins (and the changelog is the bug).

The P2 features from the November 2026 audit (M10 to M18). Each one is covered by specs that run real SQL against PGlite (test/pglite.integration.spec.ts), and the controller factory, scoping, locking, OpenAPI document, counts and quantified filters also run over real HTTP in the example app.

- Relations on writes. create, update, upsert, restore and every mass write take options.relations and options.counts and return the rows with them loaded, through the same batched loaders as a read: one query per relation for the whole batch. Ten rows from massCreate with relations: ['author'] cost one INSERT and one SELECT.
- Nested create. With a relation listed in the new writableRelations allowlist, a create body can carry it: an array for a has-many (one multi-row INSERT), an object for a belongs-to (inserted first, its key set on the row), and ids or objects for a many-to-many (new targets in one INSERT, links in one more). Everything runs in one transaction and needs RETURNING.
- attach, detach and sync for many-to-many relations: attach(id, 'tags', [1, 2]). Set based (a fixed number of statements whatever the number of ids), already-linked ids are skipped, and an unknown or soft-deleted target is a 400 with a 404 entry per id. Each returns the row with the relation loaded.
- createCrudController(Service, options), a controller factory. It registers list (offset, or keyset with?cursor=), trash, get, create, update, delete, soft delete, restore and four bulk routes, all through parseQuery. The:id param is parsed from the primary key column (ParseIntPipe for an integer, ParseUUIDPipe for a uuid) unless idType says otherwise. Routes can be turned on or off one by one and take their own decorators, so guards and roles fit in. Bulk routes are off by default. service.parseId(raw) and service.idKind() are public.

- Tenant and ownership scoping. scope: (ctx) = ({ tenant_id: ctx.tenantId }) (or a fixed object) is ANDed into every read, count, cursor page, countBy, fullTextSearch, relation count, write, bulk write, upsert, soft delete, restore, force delete and attach/detach/sync, and written onto every row a create or upsert inserts (and onto nested child rows that have the column). Another tenant's id is a 404 everywhere. The context comes from options.context or from CrudContext.run(...) / CrudContext.middleware(...), which keep it in AsyncLocalStorage for the request. - Module-level events. hooks.enableGlobalHooks: true now does what it says: every service raises a before and an after event on the injectable CrudEventBus for each write, bulk and upsert included. Subscribe with hooks.subscribers in forRoot or by injecting the bus. A bulk call raises one event with bulk: true and every id, so audit trails and cache busting stay set based. A before listener that throws stops the write; an after listener that throws inside a transaction rolls it back. skipEvents: true opts a call out.

An update, soft delete, restore or delete that names a stale version (options.expectedVersion, or the version key in an update body) is a 409 StaleVersionException. Mass writes take expectedVersions: { [id]: version } and report a 409 entry per stale id.
- Relation counts and grouped counts. options.counts: ['posts'] (or { posts: { status: 'published' } }) puts _count: { posts: 3 } on every row of find, findOne, findAll, findByCursor and the writes above, with one GROUP BY query per relation for the whole result. Soft-deleted related rows are not counted. countBy(column, filters) returns [{ value, count }], largest group first, for a column of the table or of a top-level belongs-to.

- findAll is overloaded on withCount. With a literal withCount: false it returns UncountedCrudPage (total: null), without one CrudPage (total: number), and with a withCount typed as boolean (which ParsedCrudQuery.pagination is) total is number null. Code that passes q.pagination from parseQuery straight to findAll and then does arithmetic on total needs a total!== null check. The runtime result is unchanged unless withCount: false is passed.

- Writes read options.relations and options.counts. They used to be ignored on create, update, upsert and the mass writes. They are now checked against the allowlists (with select and search) before anything is written, and loaded onto the result.
- A relation filter can name a relation of the related table, and a collection filter whose keys are all some, none or every is a quantifier. Both used to be a 400 ("Unknown filter column"). A related table that really has a column called some, none or every keeps the old meaning.
- DRIZZLE_CRUD_CONFIG.hooks carries only enableGlobalHooks (a boolean); subscribers stay on the raw config.

The P1 features from the November 2026 audit. Every one is covered by specs that run real SQL against PGlite (test/pglite.integration.spec.ts) and by e2e specs over real HTTP in the example app.

- A query string parser. service.parseQuery(query) and the standalone parseCrudQuery(query, table, options) turn?age[gte]=18&status=active&region[name]=Asia&or[0][code]=IN&sortBy=-name&page=2&limit=20&fields=id,name&with=region&search=jo into { filters, pagination, options, isCursor }. Values are coerced by Drizzle column type: integers and other numbers to number, bigint to bigint, booleans, dates to Date (an invalid one is a 400), numeric checked and kept as an exact string, and text, uuid and enum left as strings. An unknown column, relation, operator, sort column, fields entry or with path is a 400. It reads both Express 5's flat age[gte] keys and qs nested objects.
- Per-entity allowlists. filterableColumns, sortableColumns, selectableColumns, searchableColumns and loadableRelations limit what a caller may filter, sort, select, search and eager-load; writableColumns limits what create, update and upsert may write. Anything outside a set list is a 400, in the service and in the parser. Unset lists allow everything. skipAllowlists: true skips them for a trusted call, and findOne where keys are not checked.
- Trash view and purge. withDeleted: true and onlyDeleted: true work on every read (find, findOne, findAll, findByCursor, count, exists, fullTextSearch). forceDelete(id) and massForceDelete(ids) hard-delete rows whether they are soft-deleted or not.
- Upsert. upsert(dto, { conflictTarget, update }) and massUpsert(rows,...) insert or update in one statement: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE on Postgres, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE on MySQL. A clash on another unique key is a 409, bad input a 400, and the same key twice in one massUpsert (21000) a 400.
- and, or and not filter groups. { or: [{ status: 'a' }, { author: { name: 'Bob' } }], not: { tags: { name: 'x' } } }. Groups nest, hold column, relation and collection filters, work inside a relation filter, and apply to count.
- New filter operators. notIn, between, startsWith, endsWith and contains (escaped, case-insensitive unless sql.caseSensitive is on), iStartsWith, iEndsWith and iContains (always case-insensitive), and on PostgreSQL arrayContains, arrayOverlaps and jsonContains. A pattern operator on a non-text column, an array operator on a non-array column, or a PostgreSQL only operator on MySQL is a 400.
- Keyset pagination. findByCursor(filters, { cursor, limit, sortBy, count }, options) returns { data, limit, nextCursor, total? }. The cursor is base64url JSON of the last row's sort values plus the primary key, so pages stay stable under inserts and deep pages cost the same as the first. It works with every sort, filter, relation and select, keeps timestamp microseconds and follows the database's NULL ordering. The count only runs with count: true. A cursor that is not valid, or was made for another sort, is a 400.
- Multi-column and relation sorts from the caller. sortBy takes a list: ['region.name', '-name'] or [{ column, order }], and a comma separated string means the same. A dotted entry sorts by a top-level belongs-to column, joined for the data query only. A collection column is a 400.
- bulkMode: 'perItem' keeps the 3.3 behaviour of one single-row call per item, in its own savepoint.
- New exports: parseCrudQuery, and the types CrudFilter, FilterGroup, FilterOperators, FilterOperator, FilterScalar, ColumnFilter, SortInput, CursorPaginationOptions, CursorPage, CrudAllowlists, UpsertOptions, BulkMode, ParseCrudQueryOptions and ParsedCrudQuery. The Drizzle helpers between, not and notInArray are re-exported.
These change behaviour that existing code may rely on. Check each one before upgrading.

- Mass writes are set-based. massUpdate, massSoftDelete, massRestore and massDelete cost one SELECT that checks every id plus one UPDATE or DELETE... WHERE id IN (...), and massCreate one multi-row INSERT, instead of one or two queries per id. The BulkOperationException body is unchanged: when the statement fails, the batch is replayed item by item inside a savepoint that is rolled back, only to name the failing items. Hooks still run once per item, but the after hooks now run once the whole set is written instead of after each item. Duplicate ids are written once. Pass bulkMode: 'perItem' for the old behaviour.
- Create and update ignore the columns the package manages. Without writableColumns, the soft delete column is dropped from a create or update body, and the primary key and the createdAt column from an update body. An update whose only key was one of these is now a 400 ("there are no columns to update"). To write them on purpose, list them in writableColumns.
- PaginationOptions.sortBy is SortInput (string Array<string SortColumn ). Code that passes a string is unaffected; code that reads sortBy back as a string needs a narrowing check.
- between is an operator now. { col: { between: [a, b] } } used to be a 400 ("Unknown filter operator").
- buildOrderBy takes a SortInput, and buildFilterConditions and buildCollectionFilter take an optional options argument, for subclasses that call them.

- Mass operations cost a fixed number of queries (BUG-16). massUpdate over 10 ids was 20 queries; it is now 2.
- The soft delete guide's trash and purge recipes work (BUG-17). They used raw Drizzle because findAll({ deleted_at: { isNotNull: true } }) always returned nothing; the guide now uses onlyDeleted and forceDelete.
Fixes from the November 2026 audit. Every fix below is proven by a spec that runs real SQL against PGlite (test/pglite.integration.spec.ts) and failed before the change.

- String filters on integer, uuid and enum columns no longer return a 500. Query strings send every value as text, and with the default caseSensitive: false a filter such as { author_id: '1' } became lower(author_id), which Postgres rejects. lower() now only wraps text, varchar and char columns; every other column compares with = and Postgres casts the value. Relation and collection filters get the same fix.
- Date strings work on date and timestamp columns. { publishedAt: { gt: '2024-01-01' } } used to crash inside the driver (value.toISOString is not a function). The string is now turned into a Date; a value that is not a date is a 400.
- A soft-deleted belongs-to parent is no longer returned. The LEFT JOIN for an eager load or a relation filter now carries deleted_at IS NULL in its ON clause, so the parent comes back as null and { author: { name: 'Bob' } } does not match a deleted author.
- findOne can no longer hand back an arbitrary row. findOne({ email: undefined }) used to run LIMIT 1 with no condition and return the first row in the table. It is now a 400, as is a key that is not a column. null now means IS NULL instead of being skipped. An operator object works as it does in findAll.
- A soft-delete or timestamp column the table does not have is caught at startup. With camelCase keys (deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at')) the default config used to break every read with a SQL syntax error, and updatedAt silently never moved. The service now throws when it is built, naming the key to use: softDelete.column is "deleted_at", but the table has no column under that key. The column "deleted_at" is declared under the key "deletedAt"; set softDelete.column to "deletedAt".
- One bad item in a bulk call no longer fails every item after it. Each item now runs in its own savepoint, so massCreate([ok, duplicate, ok, ok]) reports the duplicate alone instead of two more 25P02 "current transaction is aborted" errors. The whole call still rolls back. The items still run one query (or two) at a time; set-based bulk writes are planned separately.
- Bulk errors reach the HTTP response. BulkOperationException now answers with { statusCode, error, message, errors: [{ index id, status, message }] }, one entry per failed item with the status that item alone would have produced. An error that is not an HTTP exception shows as status: 500 with a generic message, so SQL never leaks.
- { isNull: false } means IS NOT NULL. The value used to be ignored. isNull and isNotNull also accept the strings "true" and "false"; anything else is a 400.
- Filters the package does not understand are rejected instead of dropped. A new eq operator is supported, a Date value is an equality match instead of an empty operator object, and an unknown column, relation column or operator is a 400. Each of these used to return every row.
- Bad input is a 400 on reads too. Postgres 22P02 (wrong type, unknown enum label), 22007 and 22008 (bad dates) now map to ValidationFailedException on every path, including find, findAll, count and fullTextSearch. fullTextSearch checks its column names (an unknown one used to be a SQL syntax error), and update with nothing to set is a 400 instead of a raw "No values to set".
- fullTextSearch always paginates. Without a pagination argument it returned every match while the envelope said limit: 20. The resolved page and limit now always apply, and the data and count queries run together.
- A partial pagination override keeps the other half. pagination: { defaultLimit: 5 } used to replace the whole object, leaving maxLimit undefined and the query with no limit at all. softDelete, timestamps, pagination and sql now merge one level deep at every config layer: forRoot defaults, @CrudService, forFeature and the service constructor.
- Search and the ilike operator emit LIKE on MySQL, which has no ILIKE. MySQL's default collations already compare case-insensitively.
- Pages are stable. The primary key is now always the last ORDER BY column, so rows that tie on the sort columns, or a list with no sort at all, can no longer repeat or skip between pages.
- A row lock works with an eager belongs-to. Locks are now FOR UPDATE OF <base table (and the same for share and no key update). Postgres used to refuse with FOR UPDATE cannot be applied to the nullable side of an outer join.
- Nested collections key on their own table. A nested has-many or many-to-many used the root service's primaryKey as its default parentKey, so a root keyed on uid loaded author.posts as []. A nested level now defaults to its host table's own primary key column.
- Types in public signatures are exported. PaginationOptions, OperationOptions, SqlSearchOptions, SqlSearchMode and BulkOperationResult come from the package root, along with the new CrudFeatureConfig and BulkOperationItemError.
- CrudFeature.config is typed as CrudFeatureConfig instead of Record<string, any, so a typo in a key no longer compiles.

The same goes for an unknown column inside a relation or collection filter, and for an unknown operator. null and undefined values are still skipped.

Added. - Has-many relations, eager loaded without N+1. Declare relations: { states: { table: states, type: 'hasMany', foreignKey: 'country_id' } } and pass options.relations: ['states'] to find, findOne or findAll. Each has-many relation costs exactly one extra query for the whole result set (WHERE country_id IN (...)) no matter how many parent rows come back, and the relations run concurrently. A page of 50 countries with their states is 3 queries: data, count, children. A parent with no children gets [], never undefined. See Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations).
- Many-to-many through a join table. Declare { table: tags, type: 'manyToMany', through: countryTags, throughLocalKey: 'country_id', throughForeignKey: 'tag_id' } and the collection loads in one batched query per relation (SELECT... FROM country_tags JOIN tags... WHERE country_id IN (...)). The join-table key is used to group the rows and stripped before they are returned.
- Nested relations, any depth, with a dotted path. Put a relations map on a relation and address it with options.relations: ['states', 'states.cities'] or ['state.country']. Each nesting level costs one more batched query for the whole level, so a page of 50 countries with their states and every state's cities is 4 queries. Asking only for state.country pulls in state automatically.
- orderBy on a collection relation. { type: 'hasMany', foreignKey: 'country_id', orderBy: [{ column: 'name', order: 'asc' }] } orders the children in SQL. An unknown column is warned about and skipped, as with defaultSort.
- Collections are never joined. Filtering by a child column (findAll({ states: { name: 'Kerala' } }), findAll({ tags: { name: 'himalayan' } })) compiles to countries.id IN (SELECT... WHERE...), so parent rows are never duplicated and total and pagination stay correct. Belongs-to relations keep using a LEFT JOIN.
- options.select now narrows relation columns with a dotted path, at any depth. select: ['id', 'name', 'region.code', 'states.cities.name'] projects only those columns, for the base table, a joined belongs-to relation and a batched collection alike. Listing only relation columns leaves the parent row complete. The parent key, the child foreign key and any key a nested level needs are added back automatically, because the grouping needs them. See Column selection (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/column-selection).

ILIKE interprets %, _ and \ in the value as wildcards / escapes, so an equality filter silently became a LIKE pattern and returned non-matching rows (e.g. { title: "a_b" } matched "aXb"; { title: "a%" } matched everything). It now compiles to lower(column) = lower(value), so those characters are treated as literal data. The explicit { like } / { ilike } operators are unchanged for intentional pattern matching.

Return only the columns you need with options.select, including dotted paths that narrow eager-loaded and nested relations.

Pass options.select with the column names you want and the query stops being SELECT. It works on find, findOne and findAll, and a dotted entry narrows an eager-loaded relation.

Omit select and every column comes back, which is the default.

chunks.h: Which columns can I ask for?
chunks.t:
Entry Meaning 
--- --- 
'name' A column on this entity's table. 
'region.code' The code column of the eager-loaded region relation. 
'states.name' The name column of every child in the has-many states relation. 
'states.cities.name' The name column at the next nesting level down. Paths can be any depth. 

A dotted entry only takes effect when the relation is also listed in options.relations. Names that do not match a real column are ignored rather than rejected, so a typo returns fewer columns instead of an error. Two things make them a 400 instead: a selectableColumns allowlist (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) that does not list the name, and parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing), which checks every?fields= entry.

Two keys are added back automatically, because the loader cannot group children without them:

- the parent key on the base row (the configured primaryKey, or parentKey when set),
- the foreign key on each child row.

So select: ['name', 'states.name'] still returns id on the country and country_id on each state. The same applies at every nesting level: select: ['name', 'states.name', 'states.cities.name'] keeps states.id too, because the cities load needs it. Everything else you did not ask for is left out of the SQL.

chunks.h: Listing only relation columns keeps the parent whole
chunks.t:
If every entry is dotted, the base row is not narrowed at all:

That way select: ['region.name'] reads as "narrow the region", not "drop every country column".

- Wide tables. Skipping a large text or jsonb column you do not render is the cheapest win available.
- List endpoints. A table view usually needs three columns out of fifteen.
- Hot paths. Less data over the wire, less to hydrate, and a covering index can serve the whole query.

Keep it out of write paths: create, update and restore return the full row through RETURNING, and select does not apply to them.

- exists(id) already uses this internally, selecting only the primary key.
- Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations) covers eager loading and the batched has-many query.
- Pagination and sorting (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting) covers the rest of the read options.

SqlCrudConfig and DrizzleCrudConfig: the two interfaces that drive the module.

The package exposes two config types: DrizzleCrudConfig (the input to forRoot / forRootAsync) and SqlCrudConfig (the merged, per-entity config the base class actually uses).
The input to DrizzleCrudModule.forRoot(config) and forRootAsync. It describes the project-level configuration: the database connection, schema, and global defaults.

sql.jsonSupport, sql.enableFullTextSearch and primaryKeyType are deprecated. Nothing reads them, so they have no effect. They are still accepted so existing configs compile, and will be removed in the next major version. hooks.enableGlobalHooks was deprecated in 3.3.1 and does something again since 3.5.0: it turns on write events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events).

The fully-resolved, per-entity configuration. The package constructs this by layering:

softDelete, timestamps, pagination and sql merge one level deep at every layer, so each layer only names the settings it changes. Any other key replaces the value from the layer before. When the service is built it checks that the softDelete.column and timestamps keys exist on the table, and throws with the key to use if one does not.

The allowlists are described in Allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists). Arrays replace, they do not merge, across the config layers. scope is on Multi-tenancy (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy), versionColumn on Optimistic locking (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/optimistic-locking) and events on Global hooks and write events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events). A versionColumn or a fixed scope key that is not a column fails at startup.

createCrudController builds a NestJS controller with list, cursor, get, create, update, delete, soft delete, restore, trash and bulk routes from a service, with the right id pipe.

createCrudController(Service, options) returns a NestJS controller class whose routes call the service: list (offset and cursor), get, create, update, delete, soft delete, restore, trash and four bulk routes. It picks the id pipe from the primary key column, so you no longer copy the same controller for every entity.

Every route goes through the service, so allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists), scope (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy), soft delete, optimistic locking (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/optimistic-locking) and events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events) apply exactly as they do in code.

Route Method and path Calls Default 
--- --- --- --- 
list GET / findAll, or findByCursor when?cursor= is present on 
trash GET /trash findAll with onlyDeleted on 
get GET /:id find, 404 when missing on 
create POST / create on 
update PATCH /:id update on 
delete DELETE /:id delete, or softDelete with deleteMode: 'soft' on 
softDelete POST /:id/soft-delete softDelete on 
restore POST /:id/restore restore on 
bulkCreate POST /bulk massCreate, body is an array off 
bulkUpdate PATCH /bulk massUpdate, body is { ids, data } off 
bulkDelete POST /bulk-delete massDelete, or massSoftDelete with deleteMode: 'soft', body is { ids } off 
bulkRestore POST /bulk-restore massRestore, body is { ids } off 

The list route runs the whole query string through parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing), so filters, sortBy, fields, with, counts, withCount and cursor all work. get, create, update, restore and the bulk writes read?with=,?fields= and?counts= and ignore the rest of the query. On an entity without soft delete, trash, softDelete, restore and bulkRestore answer 404. Static paths (/trash, /bulk) are registered before /:id, so they never match as an id.

From the primary key column at request time, the way the matching Nest pipe would:

Primary key column Parsing Bad input 
--- --- --- 
integer, serial ParseIntPipe 400 Validation failed (numeric string is expected) 
uuid ParseUUIDPipe 400 
bigint in bigint mode digits only, then BigInt 400 
anything else the string as is none 

The service exposes this as service.parseId(raw) and service.idKind(), which you can use in your own controllers. Set idType: 'int' 'uuid' 'string' to fix the pipe when the class is built instead; it then shows on the route as a normal @Param('id', ParseIntPipe).

chunks.h: How do I validate request bodies?
chunks.t:
Pass the DTO classes in dto. They become the parameter types of create and update, so a global ValidationPipe validates them as usual, and bulkCreate validates each element with ParseArrayPipe({ items: dto.create }):

Without dto, bodies reach the service unvalidated; writableColumns (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) still applies.

c.s: app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true, transform: true }));

chunks.t: true or false switches a route; an object can also carry decorators for that route alone.

chunks.h: How do I add guards, interceptors or Swagger tags?
chunks.t: decorators applies method decorators to every route, before the per-route ones. classDecorators decorates the generated class. Or decorate your subclass directly:

Option Default Notes 
--- --- ---

deleteMode 'hard' 'soft' makes DELETE /:id and POST /bulk-delete move rows to the trash.

chunks.h: Can I add my own routes?
chunks.t:
Yes. The factory returns a class, so extend it and add methods. The service is on this.service:

To replace a generated route, turn it off in routes and declare your own with the same path. Do not override a generated method by name: the route metadata sits on the generated handler, so the override would not be routed.

findByCursor pages with WHERE (sort columns) > (last row) instead of OFFSET: constant cost on deep pages, stable under inserts, with an opaque nextCursor.

findByCursor(filters, pagination, options) returns a page plus an opaque nextCursor; pass that cursor back to get the next page. Each page is a WHERE on the sort columns instead of an OFFSET, so page 500 costs the same as page 1 and a row inserted on an earlier page does not shift the next one.

chunks.h: What does a page look like?
chunks.t: There is no page number: a cursor is a position, not an index. The count query is skipped unless you pass count: true, because counting is the slow part of a large list.

Field Default Notes 
--- --- --- 
cursor none The nextCursor of the previous page. Absent, null or "" means the first page. 
after none Alias of cursor. 
limit defaultLimit Capped at maxLimit. 
sortBy, sortOrder defaultSort, then the primary key Same shapes as findAll, relation columns included. See Pagination & sorting (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting). 
count false Also run the count query and return total. 

Filters, options.search, select, relations, soft delete scope and locks all work as they do in findAll.

It holds the sort values of the last row on the page, primary key last, as base64url JSON, plus the sort it was made for. The next query asks for rows after that position:

The primary key tiebreaker makes every position unique, so no row is repeated or skipped. One extra row is fetched to know whether there is a next page. NULLs follow the database's own ordering (last ascending and first descending on Postgres), and timestamp values keep their microseconds.

The cursor is opaque but not secret: anyone can decode it, so it only ever holds values the rows already show. A cursor that is not valid, or was made for a different sort, is a 400.

ORDER BY views ASC, id ASC
LIMIT 51

chunks.h: When should I use offset instead?
chunks.t: When the UI shows page numbers or jumps to page 7. Keyset pages only go forward from a known position. For infinite scroll, exports, sync jobs and any list that grows while people read it, use the cursor.

The empty-subclass pattern, generics, and how to add custom methods without breaking the framework wiring.

The SqlBaseCrudService base class is designed so the vast majority of services are empty subclasses. The connection, dialect, table, and per-entity configuration are all injected by forFeature. Your service file usually contains no logic.
The three remaining generics default to Partial:

When you want to decouple your input shape from your entity (recommended for public APIs):

The FilterDto is not used to auto-build a query. It's the type
signature of the findAll filter argument. Use it to constrain which
columns can be filtered from controllers. See
Filtering (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering) for the actual filter syntax.

Override nothing. Just add your own methods. They have full access to this.config (the resolved SqlCrudConfig) and this.config.db (the Drizzle instance), so anything you can do in raw Drizzle is available inside the service.

A common mistake is to add a constructor to inject the Drizzle instance:

The module constructs the service for you with the correct config. If you need the Drizzle instance inside a custom method, use this.config.db. It points to the same instance.

Adding a constructor that calls super({... }) is a legacy pattern. The
modern pattern is an empty subclass plus forFeature({ service, table }).
The service class itself doesn't need to know about the database or the
table.
forFeature registers the service as a Nest provider automatically. Adding @Injectable() is harmless but redundant.

chunks.h: Don't add `OnModuleInit` to "warm up" the connection
chunks.t: DrizzleCrudModule handles connection lifecycle. The connection is established lazily on first query.

chunks.h: When the empty-subclass pattern isn't enough
chunks.t:
Reach for these when the pattern breaks down:

- You need a service that queries across multiple tables. Don't try to glue this onto SqlBaseCrudService. Write a normal Nest service that injects DRIZZLE_DB and uses raw Drizzle.
- You need streaming rows. findAll materializes the result. For large result sets, inject DRIZZLE_DB and use Drizzle's streaming APIs.
- You need GraphQL resolvers. The service methods are plain async functions and can be called from any resolver layer.

HTTP status code mapping for every exception thrown by SqlBaseCrudService, with the per-method reference.

Every exception in nestjs-drizzle-crud extends @nestjs/common's HttpException. Nest's default exception filter maps the subclass to an HTTP status code automatically. No configuration required. You can instanceof the exports in a custom exception filter and the mapping will hold.

HTTP Exception When 
--- --- --- 
404 Not Found EntityNotFoundException update, restore, massUpdate, massRestore when the row doesn't exist (or is soft-deleted, when soft-delete is enabled). 
409 Conflict DuplicateEntityException create, update when a unique constraint is violated (Postgres SQLSTATE 23505). 
409 Conflict StaleVersionException Optimistic locking (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/optimistic-locking): update, softDelete, restore or delete named a version the row is no longer at. In a bulk call it is a 409 entry of the 400. 
403 Forbidden MissingScopeException A scoped entity (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy) was used without the context value its scope needs, such as no tenant on the request. 
409 Conflict EntityInUseException delete blocked because other rows still reference this one (23503, with ON DELETE RESTRICT or NO ACTION). 
400 Bad Request ForeignKeyViolationException create, update referencing a parent row that does not exist (23503). The message names the offending column. 
400 Bad Request ValidationFailedException A value the column cannot take: too long (22001), a failed check (23514), out of range (22003), the wrong type such as "abc" for an integer or an unknown enum label (22P02), or a bad date (22007, 22008), or the same key twice in one massUpsert (21000). Also an update with no column to set, a column outside writableColumns, and whatever your validateCreate / validateUpdate hooks throw. 
400 Bad Request BulkOperationException Any bulk method whose transaction rolled back. The body lists each failed item, see Bulk operations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/bulk-operations#what-does-a-failed-bulk-call-return-over-http). 
400 Bad Request BadRequestException Bad pagination, sort, filter or search input: an unknown filter column or operator, an operator on the wrong column type, an invalid date, an invalid cursor, a findOne with no condition, an unknown fullTextSearch column, anything outside an allowlist (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists), and anything parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing) cannot read. See Pagination & sorting, Clamping & fail-fast (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting#clamping-fail-fast).

DatabaseConnectionException and TransactionException are still exported but deprecated: nothing in the package throws them. A failed transaction rejects with the error that caused it.

All of them are re-exported from the package root. See Exports (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/exports).

Reads: never throw `EntityNotFoundException`. find, findOne, findAll, exists, count, and fullTextSearch return null / false / empty for missing rows. They never throw EntityNotFoundException. Callers decide how to respond.

Bad input on a read is a 400, the same as on a write. find('abc') on an integer key, findAll({ status: 'archived' }) when the enum has no such label, or { createdAt: { gte: 'garbage' } } all return 400 instead of a raw 500.

A "missing" row includes soft-deleted rows when soft-delete is enabled.

--- --- --- ---

upsert(dto, upsert) unique violation on another key hook rejection, missing FK target, unknown conflict target 
update(id, dto) row missing, soft-deleted or outside the scope unique violation, stale version hook rejection, missing FK target, nothing to update 
delete(id) row missing or soft-deleted still referenced by other rows 
forceDelete(id) row missing still referenced by other rows 
softDelete(id) row missing or soft-deleted 
restore(id) row missing 
attach / detach / sync row missing unknown target ids (404 entries), not a many-to-many

Every bulk method (massCreate, massUpdate, massSoftDelete, massRestore, massDelete, massForceDelete, massUpsert) runs in a single transaction. Any failure throws BulkOperationException (→ 400) and rolls back the entire operation. No partial writes. The response body lists each failed item as { index id, status, message }, and the exception's errors field keeps the original errors for logging.

Wraps a callback in a transaction. On any throw inside the callback, the transaction rolls back and the same error propagates unchanged. Pass { transaction: tx } in the options of any CRUD method to enlist it.

Because the exceptions extend HttpException, custom filters only need to handle the typed subclass:

If you don't write a custom filter, Nest's default filter already maps the subclass to the status code. You get correct 404 / 409 / 400 / 500 out of the box.

Turn on hooks.enableGlobalHooks and subscribe to CrudEventBus for before and after events on every write, bulk and upsert included. For audit trails and cache busting.

With hooks.enableGlobalHooks: true, every service raises a before event and an after event for each write on a module-level CrudEventBus: create, update, upsert, soft delete, restore, delete, attach, detach and sync, with each mass write raising one pair for the whole batch. Subscribe once and you see every entity, which is what an audit trail or a cache needs.

chunks.h: How do I subscribe from a provider?

Inject CrudEventBus and call subscribe. It returns a function that unsubscribes:

Writing through event.transaction puts the audit row in the same transaction as the write, so both commit or both roll back. In forRootAsync the factory can return hooks.subscribers built from injected services.

chunks.h: What does a subscriber look like?
chunks.t:
Every method is optional:

Method Called for 
--- --- 
beforeWrite, afterWrite every operation 
beforeCreate, afterCreate create, massCreate 
beforeUpdate, afterUpdate update, massUpdate 
beforeUpsert, afterUpsert upsert, massUpsert 
beforeSoftDelete, afterSoftDelete softDelete, massSoftDelete 
beforeRestore, afterRestore restore, massRestore 
beforeDelete, afterDelete delete, forceDelete, massDelete, massForceDelete 
beforeAttach / afterAttach, beforeDetach / afterDetach, beforeSync / afterSync the many-to-many link methods 

entities: ['posts', 'authors'] limits a subscriber to those table names. Listeners run in the order they subscribed and are awaited.

chunks.h: How do bulk writes raise events?
chunks.t: Once per call, with bulk: true, all the ids in ids and every written row in rows. A massUpdate of 500 rows is two events, not a thousand. With bulkMode: 'perItem' each item goes through the single-row method, so you get one pair of events per item with bulk: false.

chunks.h: Can a listener stop a write?
chunks.t: A before listener that throws stops it: nothing is written and the caller gets the error (a Nest HttpException keeps its status). An after listener that throws inside a transaction rolls the write back. Every mass write runs in a transaction; a single write only does when you pass one in options.transaction.

chunks.h: How do events relate to the per-service hooks?
chunks.t:
They are separate and both run. The protected hooks on a service (beforeCreate, afterUpdate,...) keep working as before and still follow options.hooks.skipBefore / skipAfter. Events follow options.skipEvents instead, so skipping a hook never silently skips the audit trail. See Hooks and validation (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/hooks-validation).

With enableGlobalHooks off (the default) no events fire, and the module warns at startup if hooks.subscribers is set anyway.

chunks.h: How do I use events without the module?
chunks.t: Pass a bus in the config when you build a service by hand, as in tests:

- → Bulk operations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/bulk-operations)

Build filter objects for findAll() and count(): bare values, arrays, operators such as gte, between, notIn and contains, or / and / not groups, and relation filters.

findAll(filters) and count(filters) accept a plain object keyed by column name. null and undefined values are skipped, so a query DTO with empty fields can go straight in. A key that is not a column or a configured relation is a 400 (BadRequestException), the same as an unknown sortBy.

Can I pass query string values as strings?. Yes. HTTP query values always arrive as strings, and the package handles that per column type:

- Text columns (text, varchar, char) compare case-insensitively with lower(column) = lower(value) when sql.caseSensitive is false, the default.
- Integer, uuid, enum and other non-text columns compare with a plain =, and Postgres casts the string to the column type. { author_id: '1' } matches author_id = 1.
- Date and timestamp columns turn the string into a Date first, so { createdAt: { gte: '2025-01-01' } } works. A string that is not a date is a 400.

A value the column cannot hold, such as 'abc' for an integer or an enum label that does not exist, is a 400 too, never a raw 500.

Strings are exact, not partial. 
A bare string is an exact match. On a text column with
sql.caseSensitive set to false (the default) the package compiles it to
lower(column) = lower(value),
so the match is case-insensitive and % / _ / \ in the value are
treated as literal data, never wildcards. For partial / pattern
matching, use the explicit ilike operator with your own %
wildcards:

startsWith, endsWith and contains escape %, _ and \ for you,
so { contains: '50%' } matches the text "50%".

c.s:
await service.findAll({ name: { startsWith: 'jo' } }); // starts with "jo"
  await service.findAll({ name: { contains: 'doe' } });  // contains "doe"
  await service.findAll({ name: { ilike: 'jo%n' } });    // your own pattern

chunks.t:
For anything beyond equality, wrap the value in an object with operator keys:

Multiple operators in the same object are AND-ed together. An operator the package does not know, such as { roughly: 2 }, is a 400 rather than being dropped.

Operator SQL Notes 
--- --- --- 
eq = Exact and case-sensitive, even on text columns. 
gt / gte / lt / lte = < <= Numeric and date columns. Date strings are parsed. 
neq < Not equal. 
like LIKE Caller supplies % wildcards. 
ilike ILIKE (PostgreSQL) / LIKE (MySQL) Case-insensitive. Caller supplies %. MySQL has no ILIKE; its default collations already ignore case. 
in IN (...) The value must be an array, otherwise 400. 
notIn NOT IN (...) The value must be an array, otherwise 400. 
between BETWEEN a AND b [from, to], both inclusive. Date strings are parsed. 
isNull IS NULL / IS NOT NULL true or "true" gives IS NULL, false or "false" gives IS NOT NULL. Anything else is a 400. 
isNotNull IS NOT NULL / IS NULL The mirror of isNull. 
startsWith / endsWith / contains LIKE 'x%', '%x', '%x%' Text columns only. The value is escaped. Case-insensitive unless sql.caseSensitive is true (ILIKE on Postgres, LIKE on MySQL). 
iStartsWith / iEndsWith / iContains ILIKE (PostgreSQL) / LIKE (MySQL) Always case-insensitive, whatever caseSensitive says. 
arrayContains @ PostgreSQL array columns: the column holds every value. { tags: { arrayContains: ['a', 'b'] } }. 
arrayOverlaps && PostgreSQL array columns: the column holds at least one value. 
jsonContains @ '...'::jsonb PostgreSQL jsonb columns: { meta: { jsonContains: { plan: 'pro' } } }.
A pattern operator on a column that is not text, an array operator on a column that is not an array, or a PostgreSQL only operator on MySQL is a 400 that says so.

chunks.h: How do I OR two filters?
chunks.t:
Put them in an or array. and, or and not are group keys; each member is a full filter object, so it can hold columns, relation filters, collection filters and more groups:

Groups nest, work inside a relation filter ({ states: { or: [{ name: 'Kerala' }, { name: 'Assam' }] } }) and apply to count too. An or whose member is empty matches every row, so it adds nothing. A table column named and, or or not wins over the group key.

NOT and a missing parent. 
A belongs-to filter inside not compares against a LEFT JOIN. A row whose
parent is missing has NULL there, and NOT (NULL = 'Ann') is not true, so
{ not: { author: { name: 'Ann' } } } also leaves out rows with no author.
Add { or: [{ not:... }, { author_id: { isNull: true } }] } if you want them.

findAll and count also accept options.search when you need a user-facing
search box to combine with normal filters, pagination, sorting, relation filters,
and a correct total count.

By default, search compiles to cross-column ILIKE '%term%' checks joined by
OR (LIKE on MySQL). Empty terms and unknown column names are ignored.

For PostgreSQL full-text matching inside the findAll / count path, set
mode: 'fullText':

Use fullTextSearch() directly when ranked full-text results are the primary
operation. Use findAll(...,..., { search }) when search needs to compose with
the list endpoint's filters and count query.

chunks.h: What happens with an unknown filter key?
chunks.t:
It is rejected with a 400 (BadRequestException, message Unknown filter column: <key ). Before 3.3.1 the key was dropped, so a typo such as { titel: 'x' } returned every row. The same rule covers a column inside a relation filter ({ author: { nmae: 'Bob' } }) and an unknown operator.

The simplest controller hands the query string to parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing), which splits off pagination, sort and options, coerces the values and rejects unknown keys before any SQL runs:

Set allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) so a client can only filter on the columns you mean to expose.
findAll takes three positional arguments: filters, pagination, options. See Pagination & sorting (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting) for the full shape.

When you've declared a many-to-one relation (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations), use the relation name as a filter key. The package will join the related table for you. With soft delete on, a soft-deleted parent never matches.

Multi-level filtering works through the intermediate FK column:

chunks.h: How do I filter through several relations or quantify a collection?
chunks.t:
Nest the relations, at any depth, and use some, none or every on a has-many or many-to-many relation:

Both compile to subqueries, never joins that multiply rows. See Relation filters: paths and some, none, every (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relation-filters).

await cities.findAll({ state: { country: { code: 'IN' } } });
await authors.findAll({ posts: { none: { status: 'draft' } } });
