Bind a service to its table, and override per-entity configuration.

DrizzleCrudModule.forFeature(entities) is called inside each feature module. It binds one or more services to their tables and constructs them with the correct merged configuration.
The module registers UsersService as a provider, passing it a fully-built SqlCrudConfig derived from the global forRoot defaults + any per-entity overrides you supply here.

Anything in config overrides the project defaults for that entity. The type is CrudFeatureConfig: every SqlCrudConfig key is optional, and softDelete, timestamps, pagination and sql merge with the project defaults one level deep. pagination: { defaultLimit: 5 } keeps the project's maxLimit, and sql: { caseSensitive: true } keeps useReturning.

Field Effect 
--- --- 
primaryKey Key of the primary key column (default 'id'). 
primaryKeyType Deprecated, no effect. The key type comes from the Drizzle column. See Primary keys (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/primary-keys). 
softDelete { enabled?: boolean; column?: string }. column is the key in your Drizzle table object, 'deleted_at' by default. 
timestamps { createdAt?: string; updatedAt?: string }. Keys of the timestamp columns, 'created_at' / 'updated_at' by default. timestamps: undefined turns them off for this entity. 
pagination { defaultLimit?: number; maxLimit?: number }. Per-entity override of the global defaults.pagination; a missing key keeps the project value. 
defaultSort Ordered column list for findAll() when no sortBy is passed. 
sql Per-entity dialect tuning. 
relations Belongs-to, has-many and many-to-many relations, keyed by relation name. See Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations). 
filterableColumns, sortableColumns, selectableColumns, searchableColumns, loadableRelations What a caller may filter, sort, select, search and eager-load. Unset allows everything. See Allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists). 
writableColumns The columns create, update and upsert may write; anything else is a 400. Unset, the package ignores the columns it manages. See Allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists#which-columns-can-a-body-write-by-default).

chunks.h: Does a camelCase schema need extra config?
chunks.t:
Yes, when your keys differ from the defaults. Settings name the key in the Drizzle table object, not the database column. For deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at') and friends:

The service checks these keys at startup. A key that is not on the table stops the app with a message such as softDelete.column is "deleted_at", but the table has no column under that key. The column "deleted_at" is declared under the key "deletedAt"; set softDelete.column to "deletedAt".

chunks.h: Multiple entities in one feature module
chunks.t: Each service is registered as its own provider and is independently constructed.

c.s:
DrizzleCrudModule.forFeature([
  { service: UsersService, table: users },
  { service: PostsService, table: posts },
  { service: CommentsService, table: comments, config: { /* ... */ } },
])

chunks.t:
You can also attach per-entity config to the service class itself with the @CrudService decorator. The forFeature config field still wins when both are set. The merge order is global defaults → decorator metadata → forFeature config.

The decorator is mostly a convenience for keeping the config next to the service definition. Use forFeature config for config that's data-driven or varies per feature module.

The fully-built config for each entity is available in the DRIZZLE_CRUD_CONFIG DI token. Inject it in tests to verify the merge worked:

The injected DRIZZLE_CRUD_CONFIG is the normalized global config (the
result of applying defaults). It does not include the per-entity
overrides. To inspect a single entity's resolved config, use
DRIZZLE_DB + read it off the constructed service instance.

- → Defining services: empty subclass + custom methods (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/defining-services)
- → Reference: SqlCrudConfig type (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/config-types)

Configure the database connection once in AppModule via DrizzleCrudModule.forRoot.

DrizzleCrudModule.forRoot(config) is called once in your AppModule. It owns the database connection, exposes it globally, and closes it on application shutdown (when the module built it from a connectionString).

Field Type Description 
--- --- --- 
dialect 'postgresql' \ 'mysql' Required. Database dialect. 
connectionString string Connection string. The module builds the connection (PostgreSQL only). 
db Drizzle instance Alternatively, pass a Drizzle instance you built yourself (any dialect). 
schema Record<string, unknown Drizzle schema, used when building from connectionString. 
defaults.softDelete boolean Enable soft delete for all entities (default true). 
defaults.timestamps boolean Auto-manage created_at / updated_at for all entities (default true). 
defaults.pagination { defaultLimit?: number; maxLimit?: number } Pagination defaults (default { 20, 100 }). Set one key and the other keeps its default. 
defaults.sortOrder 'asc' \ 'desc' Opt-in default sort. Entities without an explicit defaultSort fall back to ordering by their created_at column in this direction. Omit it and findAll orders by the primary key only. 
sql { caseSensitive?, useReturning? } Dialect tuning. useReturning defaults to true for PostgreSQL, false for MySQL. Every key is optional. 
hooks.enableGlobalHooks boolean Raise a before and an after event for every write on the module's CrudEventBus (default false). See Global hooks and write events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events). 
hooks.subscribers CrudSubscriber[] Subscribers added to the bus when it is created. Only called with enableGlobalHooks: true.

Provide exactly one of connectionString or db. The module will throw
if you pass neither, or both.

If your tables have no created_at / updated_at / deleted_at columns,
set defaults: { softDelete: false, timestamps: false }. If your schema
uses camelCase keys (deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at')), set the key
names per entity in forFeature. Since 3.3.1 a service whose configured
soft-delete or timestamp key is not on its table fails at startup, and the
message names the key to use.

chunks.h: PostgreSQL: let the module build the connection
chunks.t: The module imports the postgres driver on your behalf and builds a Drizzle instance from your schema. The connection is closed automatically on app shutdown.

chunks.h: Build the connection yourself (any dialect, recommended for MySQL)
chunks.t:
If you want full control over the connection (pool size, SSL, advanced mysql2 options), or you are on MySQL, pre-build the Drizzle instance and pass it as db:

When you pass db, the module does not close the connection on
shutdown. Closing it is your responsibility, and that makes it easy to share the same
pool across other Drizzle consumers (custom services, raw queries,
migrations).

Option Default What it does 
--- --- --- 
caseSensitive false When false, bare string filter values are compiled to lower(column) = lower(value) (case-insensitive exact match). When true, bare strings use plain equality (collation-dependent). Use the explicit { like } / { ilike } operators for pattern matching. 
useReturning true (Postgres) / false (MySQL) Use RETURNING after INSERT to fetch the created row. MySQL does not support RETURNING, so leave it off. 
jsonSupport true Deprecated, no effect. Nothing reads it. It is still accepted so existing configs compile, and will be removed in the next major version. 
enableFullTextSearch false Deprecated, no effect. fullTextSearch() and search.mode: 'fullText' work on PostgreSQL whatever this is set to. Removed in the next major version. 

hooks.enableGlobalHooks is not deprecated any more: since 3.5.0 it turns on module-level write events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events). Per-service hooks run either way.

caseSensitive: false only applies lower() to text columns (text, varchar, char). A string filter on an integer, uuid or enum column is a plain =, so a query string value such as?author_id=1 works.
If your config comes from ConfigService (env validation, secrets, dynamic config), use forRootAsync (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/for-root-async) instead of forRoot.

- → forRootAsync: config from ConfigService (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/for-root-async)
- → forFeature: bind services to tables (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/for-feature)

Configure the database connection asynchronously, e.g. from ConfigService.

DrizzleCrudModule.forRootAsync(options) is the asynchronous variant of forRoot. Use it when your configuration is built at runtime, typically read from ConfigService after env validation.
The useFactory may return a Promise if you need to read from a remote source (Vault, AWS SSM, etc.) before constructing the config object.
forRootAsync exposes useFactory directly. It does not accept useClass or useExisting. If you need a class-based config, wrap it:

Use forRoot when the config object can be built statically at module-evaluation time. Use forRootAsync when any of:

- The connection string is read from process.env and you want validation via ConfigService.
- The Drizzle instance is built from config (e.g. dynamic pool size).
- You depend on another provider in useFactory (feature flags, secrets manager).

- → forFeature: bind services to tables (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/for-feature)
- → Reference: DrizzleCrudConfig type (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/config-types)

PostgreSQL tsvector / tsquery via fullTextSearch(): ranked, paginated, with a clean result envelope.

The package ships a single fullTextSearch() method on SqlBaseCrudService. It builds a to_tsvector(...) @@ plainto_tsquery(...) expression across the columns you pass, orders by ts_rank, and returns the same { data, total, page, limit } envelope as findAll.

PostgreSQL only. 
Full-text search uses PostgreSQL's tsvector and tsquery types. The
method throws if the entity's dialect is 'mysql'. There is no
MySQL-specific implementation.

Soft-delete aware. 
When soft-delete is enabled on the entity, soft-deleted rows are
excluded from both the data and the total, matching the behavior of
findAll and count.

chunks.h: Do I need to enable it?
chunks.t:
No. fullTextSearch() works on any PostgreSQL entity. The sql.enableFullTextSearch flag is deprecated and has no effect.

You do need either an english (or other language) tsvector index on the columns you're searching, or a generated tsvector column. Drizzle has helpers for both. See the Drizzle docs on full-text search (https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/full-text-search) for the schema side.

Without the pagination argument the entity's default page and limit still apply (page 1, defaultLimit rows), and the envelope reports the values that were used. Before 3.3.1 an omitted pagination returned every match while the envelope said limit: 20. The data and count queries run together.

Every name in the columns list must be a column key on the table. An unknown name, or an empty list, is a 400.

The columns are passed to a Drizzle sql template that generates:

A NULL column contributes nothing to the vector, so a row still matches on its other columns.

Since 3.1.0, findAll and count can also apply a search predicate through
options.search. This is useful for list endpoints where search must compose
with structured filters, pagination, sorting, relation filters, and the same
total query:

The options.search full-text mode is PostgreSQL-only and is not ranked. Use
fullTextSearch() when search relevance should drive ordering; use
findAll(...,..., { search }) when you need a normal list endpoint with search
folded into its filtering and count behavior.
Results are ordered by ts_rank(...) descending, then by the primary key ascending. The first result is the strongest match, and rows with the same rank keep a stable order across pages.

- No highlighting. ts_headline isn't generated. If you need highlighted snippets, write a custom method.
- No multi-language documents per row. The to_tsvector config name is fixed per call (defaults to 'english'). For multi-language content, add a language column and use a raw Drizzle call.
- No fuzzy / prefix matching. plainto_tsquery is the simplest of the tsquery constructors. Use phraseto_tsquery or to_tsquery for phrase / boolean queries via a custom method.
- MySQL is unsupported. MySQL has MATCH... AGAINST but the package doesn't generate dialect-specific full-text SQL.

1. The package version, the dialect, and the NestJS and Drizzle versions.
2. The Drizzle table definition for the entity involved, trimmed to the relevant columns.
3. The forRoot and forFeature config for that entity.

Why does `findAll` return an object instead of an array?. findAll returns { data, total, page, limit } because pagination is on by default. total comes from a second count query that applies the same filters and search, so it stays correct as you page.

Why is my `like` filter not matching anything?. like and ilike take the wildcards you supply. { name: { ilike: 'jo' } } matches the exact string jo; you want { name: { ilike: 'jo%' } }. A bare string value such as { name: 'jo' } is an exact match, and by default a case-insensitive one.

Why did my insert fail on a column that does not exist?. Soft delete and package-managed timestamps write to deleted_at, created_at and updated_at. If your tables do not have those columns, disable them: defaults: { softDelete: false, timestamps: false }. See Soft delete (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete) and Timestamps (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/timestamps).

Can I use has-many or many-to-many relations?. Not through relations. The package supports many-to-one and one-to-one (belongs-to) only. Model collections with your own method over this.config.db, which stays available for anything the base service does not cover. See Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations).

before/after hooks, validateCreate/validateUpdate, and DTO-to-entity mappers: all optional overrides.

The base class exposes a small set of protected methods you can override in your service. Each is optional and has a sensible default (no-op or pass-through).

Both validateCreate and validateUpdate may return void or throw. Any throw is propagated to the caller and aborts the write. No insert, no update.

Validation runs before beforeCreate / beforeUpdate and before
the SQL. Use it for fast, synchronous input validation. For heavier
work (DB lookups, async checks), use beforeCreate / beforeUpdate
instead. They'll run in the same code path but won't be confused with
input shape validation.

The two mapper methods let you transform the DTO into the row to persist. By default, both return a shallow copy of the input.

Mappers are the right place to:

- Normalize input (lowercase emails, trim whitespace).
- Set fields the caller can't control (status: 'pending', createdBy).
- Strip fields the DTO allows but the entity doesn't have.

Each write has a before and after pair. They fire in this order:

afterCreate receives the freshly-created row. afterUpdate and afterRestore receive the updated row. afterDelete and afterSoftDelete receive the id.

If beforeCreate returns a value, that value is used instead of the input. Returning undefined / not returning keeps the input as-is.

c.s:
validateCreate
  → mapCreateDtoToEntity
  → beforeCreate
  → SQL INSERT
  → afterCreate

Condensed, accurate package facts for code generation. Prefer these over guessing.

This page is a tight, fact-only summary designed to be read by code-generation tools. Prefer the rules and gotchas below over re-deriving them from the rest of the docs.

- Name: nestjs-drizzle-crud
- Version: 3.5.0
- License: MIT
- Peers: @nestjs/common, @nestjs/core, drizzle-orm ( =0.28.0 <1.0.0), reflect-metadata. Optional: postgres (PG) / mysql2 (MySQL), @nestjs/swagger (only for ApiCrudQuery / ApiCrudList).

chunks.h: Setup is two steps and no per-service connection wiring
chunks.t:
1. DrizzleCrudModule.forRoot({ dialect, connectionString db, schema, defaults }) once in AppModule.
2. DrizzleCrudModule.forFeature([{ service, table, config? }]) in each feature module.

- Generics order: SqlBaseCrudService. All but Entity default to Partial.
- Do not add an @Inject('DRIZZLE_DB') constructor, forFeature constructs the service for you. Adding a constructor that calls super({...}) is a legacy/manual pattern and is unnecessary.
- The table is passed in forFeature, not in the service.
- If tables lack timestamp / soft-delete columns, set defaults: { softDelete: false, timestamps: false }. softDelete.column and timestamps.createdAt / updatedAt name the key in the Drizzle table object (deletedAt for deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at')); a key the table lacks makes the service throw at startup with the key to use.
- softDelete, timestamps, pagination and sql merge one level deep across forRoot, @CrudService and forFeature: pagination: { defaultLimit: 5 } keeps maxLimit.
- findAll returns { data, total, page, limit }. Not a bare array. With { withCount: false } (or?withCount=false) it skips COUNT( ): total is null and hasMore is a boolean.
- Filter operators live inside an object value: { age: { gte: 18 } }. Operators: eq gt gte lt lte neq like ilike in notIn between isNull isNotNull startsWith endsWith contains iStartsWith iEndsWith iContains arrayContains arrayOverlaps jsonContains. startsWith / endsWith / contains escape the value and follow caseSensitive; the i forms are always case-insensitive; the array and JSON operators are PostgreSQL only.
- Groups: { or: [filterA, filterB], and: [...], not: filter }, nestable, each member a full filter (columns, relations, collections), also in count. like / ilike require caller-supplied % wildcards (ilike is LIKE on MySQL); a bare string is an exact match, case-insensitive on text columns when caseSensitive === false, and % / _ / \ in the value are literal data, never wildcards. { isNull: false } means IS NOT NULL, and "true" / "false" strings work.
- String filter values are fine on integer, uuid and enum columns (plain =), and date strings are parsed for date columns. An unknown filter key, an unknown operator or an invalid date is a 400; null / undefined values are skipped.
- findOne(where) throws a 400 when no condition is left (every value undefined) or a key is not a column; null means IS NULL.
- findAll always ends ORDER BY with the primary key, so offset pages are stable. sortBy takes one column (with sortOrder, default 'desc') or a list: ['region.name', '-name'] or [{ column, order }]; a dotted entry sorts by a top-level belongs-to column.
- findByCursor(filters, { cursor, limit, sortBy, count }) is keyset pagination: returns { data, limit, nextCursor, total? }; pass nextCursor back as cursor; count defaults to false.
- service.parseQuery(@Query() query) (or parseCrudQuery(query, table, options)) turns?age[gte]=18&region[name]=Asia&or[0][code]=IN&sortBy=-name&page=2&fields=id,name&with=region&search=x&cursor= into { filters, pagination, options, isCursor }, coercing by column type; unknown keys are a 400. withDeleted / onlyDeleted need allowTrash: true. Type the FilterDto generic as CrudFilter.
- Allowlists per entity: filterableColumns, sortableColumns, selectableColumns, searchableColumns, loadableRelations, writableColumns. Unset allows everything; anything outside a set list is a 400. findOne where keys are not checked. skipAllowlists: true for trusted calls. Without writableColumns, create/update ignore the soft delete column, and update ignores the primary key and createdAt.
- findAll and count accept options.search: { term, columns, mode? }. Default mode is 'ilike' and joins cross-column contains checks with OR; mode: 'fullText' is PostgreSQL-only. Search is applied to both data and count queries.
- delete / softDelete return boolean; update / restore return the entity and throw EntityNotFoundException (→ 404) when missing. On Postgres, restore() returns the row via RETURNING rather than re-fetching it.
- All exceptions extend @nestjs/common's HttpException, so Nest's default filter maps them to status codes automatically: 404 (not found), 409 (unique violation), 400 (validation / bad input, including Postgres 22P02 / 22007 / 22008 on reads). Custom filters can instanceof them. DatabaseConnectionException and TransactionException are deprecated; nothing throws them.
- Relations: declare in forFeature config.relations, then eager-load with options.relations: ['relName'] (a dotted path nests: ['states', 'states.cities'], ['state.country'], and the parent path is pulled in automatically).
- { table, localKey, references? } is belongs-to: LEFT JOINed into the main query, resolves to an object or null.
- { table, type: 'hasMany', foreignKey, parentKey?, orderBy? } resolves to an array.
- { table, type: 'manyToMany', through, throughLocalKey, throughForeignKey, references?, parentKey?, orderBy? } resolves to an array; the join-table key never appears in the result.
- Nested relations go in a relations map on the relation itself.
- Every collection and every nested level costs exactly ONE extra query for the whole result set, never one per row. A page of 50 countries with their states and each state's cities is 4 queries: data, count, states, cities.
- A collection is never joined. Filter via findAll({ relName: { col: value } }) with the same operators: belongs-to uses the join, has-many and many-to-many compile to parentKey IN (SELECT... WHERE...), so total and pagination stay correct. A relation filter can nest through the related table's own relations at any depth ({ state: { country: { code: 'IN' } } },?state[country][code]=IN); only the top-level belongs-to is joined, deeper levels are EXISTS. A collection value may be { some }, { none } or { every } (NOT EXISTS; every is true for a parent with no rows; some: {} = has any, none: {} = has none). filterableColumns takes the full dotted path.
- A relation missing its required keys throws when the service is constructed (nested included, with the full path in the message).
- options.select narrows the projection and accepts dotted relation paths at any depth: ['id', 'name', 'region.code', 'states.cities.name']. Unknown names are ignored. When every entry is dotted the base row is returned in full. The parent key, the child foreign key and any key a nested level needs are re-added automatically, because the grouping needs them.
- The package ships an MCP server, npx nestjs-drizzle-crud-mcp (stdio), with list_docs, get_doc and search_docs over AGENT.md / README.md / CHANGELOG.md. Rules templates for every agent: AGENTS.template.md and CLAUDE.template.md.
- Primary keys: primaryKey (default 'id') per entity in forFeature config. primaryKeyType is deprecated and has no effect. UUID works on Postgres via RETURNING; with uuid keys, route params are strings. Don't use ParseIntPipe.
- Nested collections default parentKey to their host table's own primary key, not the root service's.
- Row locks use FOR UPDATE OF <base table, so they work with an eager belongs-to.
- Full-text search is PostgreSQL-only. fullTextSearch() always applies page and limit, and rejects unknown columns with a 400. sql.enableFullTextSearch and sql.jsonSupport are deprecated no-ops.
- Bulk methods are transactional and set-based: one SELECT that checks the ids plus one INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE for the whole set. A failure throws BulkOperationException and rolls back the entire operation; its 400 body lists errors: [{ index id, status, message }] for the failed items only. bulkMode: 'perItem' runs one single-row call per item instead.
- upsert(dto, { conflictTarget, update }) and massUpsert(rows,...): ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE on Postgres, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE on MySQL. A clash on another unique key is a 409.
- A soft-deleted belongs-to parent comes back as null and never matches a relation filter. Trash: pass onlyDeleted: true (or withDeleted: true) in the options of any read. Purge: forceDelete(id) / massForceDelete(ids); delete(id) answers 404 for a row in the trash.
- executeSqlTransaction(async (tx) =...) opens a transaction; pass { transaction: tx } in options to any CRUD method to enlist it.

- Controllers: prefer class XController extends createCrudController(XService, { dto: { create, update } }) under @Controller('x') over hand-writing CRUD routes. Bulk routes are off until enabled in routes. The id is parsed from the primary key column (ParseIntPipe / ParseUUIDPipe); do not add your own pipe unless you set idType. Do not override a generated method by name; disable the route and add your own.
- OpenAPI: @ApiCrudList({ table,...entityConfig }) on a list route. Keep the entity config in one constant shared with forFeature. Needs @nestjs/swagger installed.
- Tenancy: set scope: (ctx) = ({ tenant_id: ctx.tenantId }) on the entity and provide the context with CrudContext.middleware(req = ({ tenantId })) in a module's configure, CrudContext.run(ctx, fn), or options.context. Never add a manual tenant_id filter or set it in the body: the scope is ANDed into every read and write and written on create. Another tenant's id is a 404; a missing context value is a 403 (MissingScopeException). skipScope: true only for trusted jobs. Scoped upsert is PostgreSQL only.
- Events: hooks: { enableGlobalHooks: true } in forRoot, then inject CrudEventBus and subscribe({ afterWrite(e) {...} }). One event per mass call (bulk: true). Use e.transaction to write audit rows atomically. options.skipEvents skips them; hooks.skipBefore/skipAfter do not.
- Optimistic locking: versionColumn: 'version' (integer, default 1). Clients send the version they read in the update body (or expectedVersion); a stale one is a 409 StaleVersionException. Never write the version yourself. Bulk: expectedVersions: { [String(id)]: version }.
- Relations on writes: create(dto, { relations: ['author'] }) returns the row with relations loaded (also update, upsert, restore, mass writes). Nested create needs writableRelations: ['posts']; has-many takes an array, belongs-to an object, many-to-many ids or objects; one transaction, PostgreSQL. Use attach(id, 'tags', ids), detach(id, 'tags', ids?), sync(id, 'tags', ids) for links, never raw inserts into the join table.
- Aggregates: options.counts: ['posts'] adds _count: { posts: n } with one grouped query per relation (collections only);?counts=posts from a query string. countBy('status', filters) returns [{ value, count }]; the column must be filterable.

Scope every read, count and write to a tenant or owner with one config key: scope: (ctx) => ({ tenant_id: ctx.tenantId }). Another tenant's id is a 404, and a missing tenant is a 403.

Set scope on an entity and every query the service runs is limited to the rows that match it: reads, counts, cursors, writes, bulk writes, upserts, soft deletes, restores and force deletes. A create writes the scope onto the new row. You cannot forget it in one place, because no method runs without it.

chunks.h: What does a scope look like?
chunks.t:
column: value pairs, each an exact match (null means IS NULL). Either fixed, or a function of the call's context:

Returning null leaves that call unscoped on purpose, for an admin or a background job. A key that is not a column throws. The function runs synchronously, so resolve anything async (the user, their tenant) in middleware and put the result in the context.

c.s:
scope: { region_id: 1 }                                   // fixed
scope: (ctx) => ({ tenant_id: ctx.tenantId })             // per request
scope: (ctx) => ({ tenant_id: ctx.tenantId, owner_id: ctx.userId })
scope: (ctx) => (ctx.isAdmin ? null : { tenant_id: ctx.tenantId })

chunks.h: Where does the context come from?
chunks.t:
From options.context on the call, or else from CrudContext, which keeps a per-request value in Node's AsyncLocalStorage so it follows the request through every await:

Outside a request, wrap the work yourself:

The call fails closed. When the scope function returns undefined for a column (no tenant on the request), the service throws MissingScopeException, a 403, instead of running unscoped. A trusted server-side call can opt out with skipScope: true:

c.s: await projects.count({}, { skipScope: true }); // every tenant

chunks.t:
All of them:

Area Methods Another tenant's row 
--- --- --- 
Reads find, findOne, exists, findAll, findByCursor, count, countBy, fullTextSearch, relation counts not found: null, false, or left out of the page and the total 
Single writes update, softDelete, restore, delete, forceDelete 404 
Upsert upsert, massUpsert 404 (the conflicting row is not updated) 
Bulk massUpdate, massSoftDelete, massRestore, massDelete, massForceDelete 400 with a 404 entry for that id, nothing written 
Links attach, detach, sync 404 

The scope is ANDed into the existence check and into the UPDATE or DELETE statement itself, so a row cannot change tenant between the two. On upsert it sits in the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE... WHERE, which MySQL does not have, so a scoped upsert on MySQL is a 400.

chunks.h: What does a create or update do with the scope column?
chunks.t:
create, massCreate and upsert write the scope values onto the row, over whatever the body said, so a client cannot create a row in another tenant. update never sets the scope columns: they are dropped from the SET, so a body cannot move a row to another tenant. An update whose only column was the scope column is a 400 (nothing to update).

With nested create (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations-on-writes), child rows get the scope values too when their table has the same columns, and attach only links targets in the caller's tenant when the related table has the scope column.

On reads, no. The scope applies to the service's own table; a relation loaded with relations or counted with counts follows its foreign key. That is safe when related rows always share the parent's tenant, which a foreign key usually guarantees. Give a related table its own service with its own scope when it is queried on its own.

- → CRUD controller factory (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/controller-factory)
- → Optimistic locking (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/optimistic-locking)
- → Errors: MissingScopeException and the rest (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/errors)

ApiCrudQuery and ApiCrudList document page, limit, sortBy, cursor, withCount, search, fields, with, counts and every filterable column in Swagger, from the entity's allowlists.

@ApiCrudList(source) documents a list route in Swagger: every query parameter parseQuery reads (page, limit, sort, cursor, withCount, search, fields, relations, counts) plus each filterable column with its type, and the page envelope as the 200 response. @ApiCrudQuery(source) does the parameters alone.

Only if you use these decorators. @nestjs/swagger is an optional peer dependency: the package requires it the first time one of the decorators runs, so an app without Swagger never loads it and has nothing new to install. Without it installed, applying a decorator throws an error that says so.

c.s: pnpm add @nestjs/swagger

chunks.h: What do I pass as the source?
chunks.t:
The same facts the service uses, so the docs match what the API accepts:

- A config object with the table: { table, relations, filterableColumns, sortableColumns, selectableColumns, searchableColumns, loadableRelations, allowTrash }. Keep the entity config in one constant and spread it into both forFeature and the decorator.
- A service class decorated with @CrudService({ table,... }), whose metadata already holds the table and lists. A class without that metadata throws, naming what to pass instead.

Config set only in forFeature is not visible when the decorator runs, which is why the shared constant is the usual pattern.

Parameter Documented when 
--- --- 
page, limit, sortBy, sortOrder, withCount, fields always; sortBy and fields list the sortable and selectable columns 
with, counts the entity has relations; with lists the loadable ones 
search searchableColumns (or searchColumns) is set 
cursor, count unless { cursor: false } 
withDeleted, onlyDeleted allowTrash: true, and not on a trash route ({ trash: true }) 
one parameter per filter column every entry of filterableColumns, or every column when it is unset 

A relation path is written the way a query string sends it: region.name becomes region[name]. Each filter parameter carries the column's OpenAPI type (integer, number, boolean, date-time, uuid, an enum's values) and lists the bracket operators. Every parameter is optional.

ApiCrudList adds the 200 response: { data, total, page, limit, hasMore, nextCursor }, with the row schema built from the table's columns and total marked nullable for withCount=false.

chunks.p: Optimistic locking with a version column
chunks.h: Optimistic locking with a version column
chunks.t:
Set versionColumn and a write that names a stale version is a 409 StaleVersionException. The version starts at 1 and goes up on every update, soft delete, restore, upsert and bulk write.

Optimistic locking stops a client from overwriting a change it never saw: set versionColumn, send back the version you read, and a write against a row that has moved on since is a 409. It needs no row lock, so it suits the read, edit, save flow of a form.

chunks.p: Optimistic locking with a version column
chunks.t: It starts at 1 on create (whatever the body says) and goes up by one on every write: update, softDelete, restore, an upsert that hits an existing row, and every row of massUpdate, massSoftDelete, massRestore and massUpsert. It is computed in SQL (SET version = version + 1), never taken from a body.

chunks.p: Optimistic locking with a version column
chunks.h: How do I send the version I read?
chunks.t:
Either in the body under the version column's key, which is what a REST client does with the object it fetched:

or as options.expectedVersion, which also works for the methods without a body:

options.expectedVersion wins when both are given. A version that is not an integer is a 400. The version key is removed from the body before the update, so it is never written directly, even when writableColumns is set.

c.s:
const project = await projects.find(1);              // version: 3
await projects.update(1, { name: 'New', version: 3 }); // ok, version 4
await projects.update(1, { name: 'Late', version: 3 }); // 409

chunks.p: Optimistic locking with a version column
chunks.h: What does a stale write return?
chunks.t: StaleVersionException, which extends Nest's ConflictException, so the HTTP answer is a 409 with a message telling the client to read the row again. The check runs twice: the existence check compares the version before anything is written, and the UPDATE or DELETE carries AND version = <expected, so a write that lands between the two is also caught.

chunks.p: Optimistic locking with a version column
chunks.h: What if the client sends no version?
chunks.t: Then there is no check, and the write still bumps the version. That keeps internal writes simple; require the field in your update DTO when every client must send it.

chunks.p: Optimistic locking with a version column
chunks.h: How does it work with bulk writes?
chunks.t:
Pass expectedVersions, keyed by the id as a string:

Any id at another version makes the whole call a 400 BulkOperationException with a 409 entry for that id, and nothing is written:

massSoftDelete, massRestore and massDelete take expectedVersions the same way.

The findAll() return shape, withCount: false to skip COUNT(*), default sort, and sortBy: one column, several columns, or a belongs-to relation column such as region.name.

findAll(filters?, pagination?, options?) returns a paginated result envelope, not a bare array.

The pagination argument is optional. When omitted, findAll uses
defaults.pagination.defaultLimit (default 20) and starts at page 1.
total is the row count after filters and options.search, but before
pagination, so it stays correct across pages.

Field Type Default Notes 
--- --- --- --- 
page number 1 1-indexed. 
limit number defaults.pagination.defaultLimit Capped at defaults.pagination.maxLimit (default 100). 
sortBy string \ Array<string \ SortColumn defaultSort (entity) One column, or a list. See below. 
sortOrder 'asc' \ 'desc' 'desc' Direction for a single sortBy string. 
withCount boolean true false skips the count query. See below.

chunks.h: How do I skip the count query?
chunks.t:
Pass withCount: false. findAll then runs one query instead of two, total is null, and hasMore says whether another page follows:

hasMore comes from fetching one row more than the page and dropping it, so it costs nothing extra. COUNT( ) is the expensive half of a list on a big table, and infinite scroll or a "next" button does not need it. From a query string,?withCount=false sets it.

The return type follows the option: with withCount: false written in the call, total is typed null and hasMore is a boolean; with nothing (or true), total is a number. When the value is only known at run time, as with the output of parseQuery, total is typed number null. With the count on, the envelope has no hasMore key, the same as before.

c.s:
const page = await posts.findAll({}, { page: 3, limit: 20, withCount: false });
// { data: [...20 rows], total: null, page: 3, limit: 20, hasMore: true }

chunks.t:
Explicit `sortBy`. A single string sorts by one column in sortOrder, which defaults to 'desc', as it always has.

How do I sort by several columns?. Pass a list. Each entry sorts ascending unless it starts with -; an entry can also be a { column, order } object. A comma separated string means the same list.

How do I sort by a related column?. Write it as relation.column. It works for a top-level belongs-to relation, which is joined for the data query only (the count query stays unjoined):

A has-many or many-to-many column cannot be sorted on, because a row has many of them; that is a 400. So is an unknown column, and a column outside sortableColumns (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists). Over HTTP, parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing) reads?sortBy=region.name,-name.

Why does every query end with the primary key?. So that pages are stable. Postgres returns rows that tie on the sort columns in no fixed order, and without any ORDER BY the order can change between two queries. Offset pagination over an unstable order repeats some rows and skips others. Since 3.3.1 the primary key is always the last ORDER BY column (ascending), unless it is already in the list:
A single string sorts by one column in sortOrder, which defaults to 'desc', as it always has.

Write it as relation.column. It works for a top-level belongs-to relation, which is joined for the data query only (the count query stays unjoined):

await countries.findAll({}, { sortBy: ['region.name', 'name'] });
// LEFT JOIN regions ... ORDER BY regions.name ASC, countries.name ASC, countries.id ASC

chunks.h: Why does every query end with the primary key?
chunks.t: So that pages are stable. Postgres returns rows that tie on the sort columns in no fixed order, and without any ORDER BY the order can change between two queries. Offset pagination over an unstable order repeats some rows and skips others. Since 3.3.1 the primary key is always the last ORDER BY column (ascending), unless it is already in the list:

Define an ordered list of columns in forFeature config. They're applied as the ORDER BY clause when no explicit sortBy is passed. The first column is the primary sort, the rest are tiebreakers.

sortBy replaces defaultSort. 
An explicit sortBy replaces the entity's defaultSort entirely. The
primary key tiebreaker is still added.

Set defaults.sortOrder in forRoot to apply a created_at fallback to every entity that doesn't define its own defaultSort:

Per-column order defaults to 'asc' when you don't specify it. Unknown columns in defaultSort are skipped and emit a [nestjs-drizzle-crud] defaultSort references unknown column "<col "; skipping. warning at startup. They never throw. (Caller-supplied sortBy is different: it throws on unknown columns, see below.)

limit is capped at defaults.pagination.maxLimit. Anything over the cap is silently lowered to the cap. To return more rows per page, raise the cap in forRoot:

Either key can be set on its own, at the project level or per entity. pagination: { defaultLimit: 5 } keeps maxLimit at 100. Before 3.3.1 a per-entity override with one key dropped the other, and the query ran with no limit at all.

The cap is enforced on every call. If you genuinely need to return every row
(e.g. an export endpoint), use a custom method that bypasses findAll and
calls Drizzle directly.

Pagination and sorting inputs are normalized before they reach SQL. Bad input is either silently clamped to a safe value or rejected as BadRequestException (→ 400), depending on the failure mode.

Silently clamped (never throws): 

Input Result 
--- --- 
page < 1 1 
limit <= 0 1 
limit maxLimit maxLimit 
page / limit not a finite number 1 / defaultLimit 

A LIMIT 0 or negative OFFSET can never reach SQL. Every value is clamped via the package's shared resolvePagination helper.

Throws BadRequestException (→ 400):

Input Why 
--- --- 
Caller sortBy not a column on the table (or on a belongs-to relation) Mirrors the unknown-column guard, typos surface immediately instead of returning unsorted data. 
Caller sortBy outside sortableColumns See Allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists). 
Caller sortOrder other than 'asc' / 'desc' Without the guard, anything other than 'desc' silently sorted ascending. 
{ gt / gte / lt / lte: NaN } or { …: Infinity } Reaches SQL as an opaque 500; rejected as 400 instead. 
A filter key that is not a column or relation, or an unknown operator Dropping it would return every row for a typo. See Filtering (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering#what-happens-with-an-unknown-filter-key). 
A date filter value that is not a date { createdAt: { gte: 'garbage' } }. 

For the full per-method exception table (404 / 409 / 400 / 500 mapping), see Errors (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/errors).

findAll is offset based. For deep pages, infinite scroll or lists that change while people read them, use findByCursor, which returns a nextCursor instead of a page number. See Cursor pagination (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/cursor-pagination).

- → Cursor pagination with findByCursor (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/cursor-pagination)
- → Relations: eager loading via options.relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations)
- → Bulk operations: transactional pagination-free reads (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/bulk-operations)

serial, int, bigint, bigserial, and uuid: RETURNING vs insertId, and the ParseIntPipe warning.

Each entity names its primary key in the forFeature config:

Field Default Notes 
--- --- --- 
primaryKey 'id' The key of the primary key column in your Drizzle table object. 
primaryKeyType 'serial' Deprecated, no effect. Nothing reads it: the key type comes from the Drizzle column. Still accepted so existing configs compile; removed in the next major version. 

The primary key is also the last ORDER BY column on every findAll, which keeps offset pagination stable. See Pagination & sorting (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting#why-does-every-query-end-with-the-primary-key).

The default. Use this for any numeric primary key, regardless of size:

On PostgreSQL the created row is returned via RETURNING; on MySQL the driver fills in insertId and the service re-reads the row. Both code paths produce the same Promise result.

PostgreSQL. Works fully. The created row is returned via RETURNING with the DB-generated UUID.

MySQL. MySQL has no RETURNING. The package needs to know the UUID to re-read the row. Supply the UUID in your create payload. The service will use it as the lookup key:

chunks.t: Not supported out of the box. The package assumes a single-column primary key on every CRUD method (find(id), update(id,...), etc.). For composite keys, write a custom service method that takes a structured where clause and uses raw Drizzle.

Different entities can use different key types with no extra config. The type comes from each table's Drizzle column:

A key that is not named id still needs config: { primaryKey: '<key ' }.

The CRUD methods on each service are typed against the right column shape automatically.

c.s:
DrizzleCrudModule.forFeature([
  { service: UsersService, table: users },   // serial
  { service: TagsService, table: tags },     // uuid
  { service: EventsService, table: events }, // bigserial
])

chunks.t:
- serial. Simpler, smaller index, faster joins. Predictable for debugging.
- uuid. Safer for distributed systems (no auto-increment collisions when merging data), safer for public-facing IDs (no enumeration), but larger index and slightly slower joins.

For internal entities (join tables, audit logs), serial is usually fine. For entities that get exposed in URLs or APIs to other systems, uuid is the safer default.

- → Soft delete: independent of primary key, but the restore() return type depends on it (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete)
- → Defining services: custom methods that take advantage of the typed PK (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/defining-services)

parseCrudQuery and service.parseQuery turn ?age[gte]=18&status=active&sortBy=-name&page=2 into typed filters, pagination and options, coerced by Drizzle column type.

service.parseQuery(query) turns an HTTP query string into the three arguments findAll takes, so a list endpoint is one line of controller code. Values are coerced by the Drizzle column type, and anything the table does not have is a 400.

parseQuery reads the entity's own table, relations, primary key and allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists). The standalone parseCrudQuery(query, table, options) does the same for code that has no service at hand.

chunks.h: What does the query string look like?
chunks.t:
Each filter is a key: a bare value for an exact match, or brackets for an operator. A relation name filters by a related column.

A relation filter can go on through the related table's own relations, and a collection takes some, none or every as the next key; filterableColumns is checked against the full dotted path (state.country.code). See Relation filters (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relation-filters).

Every filter operator (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering#operator-reference) works in brackets. in, notIn, between, arrayContains and arrayOverlaps take a comma separated list; use a repeated key (name[in]=a&name[in]=b) when a value contains a comma. jsonContains takes JSON: meta[jsonContains]={"size":"L"}.

The parser reads both Express 5's default flat keys (age[gte]) and the nested objects of the qs parser (app.set('query parser', 'extended')), so it works whichever one your app uses.

c.s:
GET /countries?status=active                 exact match
GET /countries?population[gte]=1000000       operator
GET /countries?region_id[in]=1,3             list operand, comma separated
GET /countries?code=IN&code=NP               repeated key: IN (...)
GET /countries?region[name]=Asia             belongs-to column (region.name=Asia works too)
GET /countries?states[name]=Kerala           has-many or many-to-many column
GET /cities?state[country][code]=IN          a path through relations (state.country.code=IN too)
GET /countries?states[none][name]=Kerala     some / none / every on a collection
GET /countries?states[some]=                 has at least one state
GET /countries?or[0][code]=IN&or[1][code]=NP OR group
GET /countries?not[region][name]=Asia        NOT group
GET /countries?sortBy=region.name,-name&page=2&limit=20
GET /countries?fields=id,name,region.name&with=region
GET /countries?search=nep
GET /countries?cursor=                       first keyset page
GET /countries?withCount=false               skip the COUNT(*)
GET /countries?counts=states,tags            _count on each row

chunks.t:
Parameter Becomes Notes 
--- --- --- 
page, limit pagination.page, pagination.limit Positive integers, otherwise a 400. limit is still capped at maxLimit. 
sortBy pagination.sortBy Comma list. -name sorts descending, name ascending, region.name sorts by a belongs-to column. 
sortOrder direction of the unprefixed sortBy entries asc or desc. 
fields options.select Comma list, dotted paths for relations. 
with options.relations Comma list of relation paths. 
search options.search Searches searchColumns, or the entity's searchableColumns. Without either it is a 400. 
cursor / after pagination.cursor Sets isCursor. Empty means the first page. See Cursor pagination (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/cursor-pagination). 
count pagination.count true asks findByCursor for a total. 
withCount pagination.withCount false makes findAll skip the count: total is null and hasMore is set. See Pagination (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/pagination-sorting#how-do-i-skip-the-count-query). 
counts options.counts Comma list of has-many or many-to-many relations to count under _count. Checked against loadableRelations; a belongs-to is a 400. See Aggregates (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates). 
withDeleted, onlyDeleted options.withDeleted, options.onlyDeleted Only with allowTrash: true; otherwise they are unknown filter columns, so a 400. See Soft delete (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete).
Every other key is a filter. To read a parameter of your own, list it in ignore and take it from the query yourself.

By the Drizzle column, so the service gets the type it expects:

Column Query value Result 
--- --- --- 
integer, serial, real, double, numeric in number mode "18" 18. Not a number: 400. 
bigint in bigint mode "9007199254740993" 9007199254740993n, exact. 
numeric / decimal in string mode "10.50" Checked as a number, kept as the exact string. 
boolean "true", "false", "1", "0" true / false. Anything else: 400. 
timestamp, date (date mode) "2025-01-01" A Date. Not a date: 400. 
text, varchar, uuid, enum "Asia" Left as a string. Postgres checks uuid and enum values, and a bad one is a 400. 
array operands "red,blue" Each element coerced by the array's element type.

The same things the service rejects, caught before any SQL runs: an unknown column, relation, operator, sort column, fields entry or with path; a value the column cannot hold; a malformed key such as ab; a key given twice where one value is expected (page=1&page=2); and anything outside an [allowlist (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists). Keys such as __proto__ are refused outright.
parseCrudQuery(query, table, options) also takes relations, primaryKey and the allowlist keys, which parseQuery fills in from the entity config.
Type the service's fourth generic as CrudFilter so the parsed filters fit without a cast:

- → Allowlists: limit what a client may filter, sort, select and write (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists)
- → Filtering: every operator, and or / not groups (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering)
- → Cursor pagination with findByCursor (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/cursor-pagination)
- → CRUD controller factory: every route wired for you (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/controller-factory)

A five-step walkthrough that takes a fresh Drizzle schema to a working CRUD controller in under five minutes.

This guide walks you through wiring a complete CRUD surface for a users table in a fresh NestJS + Drizzle project. By the end you'll have a controller exposing GET /users, GET /users/:id, POST /users, PUT /users/:id, and DELETE /users/:id, all backed by the SqlBaseCrudService base class.

The createdAt / updatedAt / deletedAt columns are conventional. The
package refers to them by their key in the table object, and its
defaults are the snake_case keys created_at, updated_at and
deleted_at. This schema uses camelCase keys, so step 4 names them. See
Timestamps (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/timestamps) and Soft delete (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete).
The module creates and owns the connection, exposes it globally, and closes it on application shutdown.

The service is an empty subclass. Do not inject the db, do not 
pass dialect or db to super(...), and do not add a
@Inject('DRIZZLE_DB') constructor, forFeature constructs the service for
you. The table is bound in forFeature, not in the service.
@Param('id', ParseIntPipe) works because the id column is serial. If you switch to a uuid primary key, remove ParseIntPipe. See Primary keys (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/primary-keys).

findOne(where, options?) Promise Equality match. A where with no usable condition is a 400.

count(filters?, options?) Promise<number

chunks.p: Relation filters, paths and some, none, every
chunks.h: Relation filters, paths and some, none, every
chunks.t:
Filter through relations at any depth (state.country.code) and quantify collections with some, none and every. Compiled to EXISTS and NOT EXISTS subqueries, so rows are never multiplied.

A relation filter can go on through the related table's own relations, to any depth, and a filter on a collection can say some, none or every. Everything below the first belongs-to join compiles to an EXISTS or NOT EXISTS subquery, so parent rows are never multiplied and total stays right.

chunks.p: Relation filters, paths and some, none, every
chunks.h: How do I filter through more than one relation?
chunks.t:
Nest the relation names, as declared in each relation's own relations config:

The top-level belongs-to (state) is joined as before. Each deeper level is a correlated EXISTS:

Each subquery gets its own table alias, so a relation back to a table already in the query (a self relation) still resolves. Soft-deleted related rows never match.

chunks.p: Relation filters, paths and some, none, every
chunks.h: How do I use some, none and every?
chunks.t:
On a has-many or many-to-many relation, the value is a filter (meaning some) or an object of quantifiers:

Filter Keeps parents that SQL 
--- --- --- 
{ posts: { status: 'draft' } } have at least one matching row id IN (SELECT...) 
{ posts: { some: { status: 'draft' } } } the same id IN (SELECT...) 
{ posts: { some: {} } } have any row at all id IN (SELECT...) 
{ posts: { none: { status: 'draft' } } } have no matching row NOT EXISTS (...)

Eager-load belongs-to, has-many, many-to-many and nested relations in Drizzle CRUD without N+1 queries, and filter by related columns.

Declare relations in the entity's forFeature config under relations, keyed by relation name, then eager-load them with options.relations. Three kinds are supported, and any of them can nest:

- belongs-to (many-to-one / one-to-one): a foreign key on this table points at another table. Loaded with a LEFT JOIN in the same query, resolves to an object or null.
- has-many (one-to-many): a foreign key on the other table points back here. Loaded with one extra batched query per relation, resolves to an array.
- many-to-many: a join table holds a foreign key to each side. Loaded with one extra batched query per relation, resolves to an array.

No shape ever runs a query per row, so eager loading a page of 50 rows costs the same number of queries as a page of 5.

chunks.h: How do I avoid N+1 queries?
chunks.t:
Ask for the relation instead of looping. find, findOne and findAll accept options.relations, and the service does the batching for you:

The alternative, fetching countries and then querying states inside a loop, is 1 + N queries. That is the pattern this replaces.

Relation type SQL Extra queries Result shape 
--- --- --- --- 
belongsTo (default) LEFT JOIN in the main query 0 object, or null when unmatched 
hasMany SELECT... WHERE fk IN (parent keys) 1 per relation, for the whole page array, [] when empty 
manyToMany SELECT... FROM join JOIN target... WHERE fk IN (parent keys) 1 per relation, for the whole page array, [] when empty 
nested (any shape) as above, against the level above it 1 per relation per level as above 

Relations load concurrently, so three collections are three parallel queries, not three round trips in sequence.

Field Type Notes 
--- --- --- 
<relationName string The key used to refer to the relation in filters and eager loads. 
table Drizzle table The target table. 
type 'belongsTo' \ 'hasMany'? Defaults to 'belongsTo'. 
localKey string The column on the current table that holds the FK. Required for belongs-to. 
references string? The column on the target table to match against. Defaults to 'id'.

Set type: 'hasMany' and name the column on the child table that points back at this one:

Field Type Notes 
--- --- --- 
foreignKey string The column on the target table pointing back here. Required for has-many. 
parentKey string? The column on the current table that foreignKey matches. Defaults to that table's primary key: the configured primaryKey at the top level, the related table's own primary key column at a nested level. 
orderBy SortColumn[]? How to order the collection, applied in SQL. 

A relation missing its key column throws when the service is constructed, so a typo shows up at startup instead of as an empty array at runtime.

Name the join table and its two foreign-key columns:

Field Type Notes 
--- --- --- 
through Drizzle table The join table. Required for many-to-many. 
throughLocalKey string The join-table column matching this table's parentKey. 
throughForeignKey string The join-table column matching references on the target table. 
references string? The target column. Defaults to 'id'. 
parentKey string? The column on the current table. Defaults to that table's primary key, as for has-many. 

Nested collections key on their own table. 
Before 3.3.1 a nested collection borrowed the root service's primaryKey.
With a root keyed on uid, comment.author.posts looked for
author.uid and came back empty. A nested level now uses the primary key
column of the table it hangs off (authors.id here), so no parentKey is
needed unless the join column is something else.

The join table never appears in the result. Its key is used to group each row onto the right parent and then removed.

chunks.h: How do I eager-load a relation of a relation?
chunks.t:
Give the relation its own relations map, then address it with a dotted path in options.relations:

Each level is one batched query for every row at that level, so 50 countries with 200 states and 900 cities is still 4 queries. Nesting works for every shape, including a belongs-to chain:

Asking for state.country pulls in state on its own, so you do not have to list both.

Set orderBy on the relation and the children come back sorted by SQL, not by insertion order:

An orderBy entry naming a column that does not exist is warned about and skipped, the same way defaultSort behaves.

An unmatched belongs-to relation comes back as null, never as an object full of nulls. A parent with no children comes back as [], so callers can iterate without a guard.

Soft delete is respected on both sides: when it is enabled and the child table has the configured column, deleted children are excluded from the collection.

chunks.h: Why is a collection not joined?
chunks.t:
Because a join would break the page. One country with four states becomes four rows, count( ) returns 4 instead of 1, and limit 50 silently cuts a country in half. The batched IN (...) query keeps one row per parent and keeps total honest. This applies to has-many and many-to-many alike.

The same reasoning applies to filters, so filtering by a child column compiles to a subquery:

That is "parents with at least one matching child". Many-to-many filters work the same way, through the join table. Both support the same operators as any other filter, and the predicate is applied to the count query too.

c.s:
// countries.id IN (SELECT country_id FROM states WHERE lower(name) = lower('Kerala'))
await countries.findAll({ states: { name: 'Kerala' } });

chunks.t: Use the relation name as a filter key with a nested object of the related table's columns:

Multi-level filtering works through the intermediate table's columns (e.g. filter cities by state.country_id), so you usually do not need a direct relation to the far table.

Or filter through the relation chain itself, { state: { country: { code: 'IN' } } }, and quantify collections with some, none and every. See Relation filters (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relation-filters).

You can also declare a direct relation to the far table if the queries are frequent. Each declared relation is joined (belongs-to) or batched (has-many) independently when it is referenced in a filter or in options.relations.

options.select takes dotted paths, so you can narrow a relation instead of hydrating every column:

The child keeps its foreign key even when you do not list it, because that column is what maps each child back to its parent. See column selection (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/column-selection) for the full rules.

- Belongs-to joins are always LEFT. Filter by id: { isNotNull: true } if you need to drop the unmatched rows.
- A collection is not paginated per parent. orderBy sorts the children, but every matching child is returned. Use a custom method when you need "the latest three per parent".
- Join-table columns are not returned. If the join table carries data of its own (a role, a position), model it as an entity with two belongs-to relations.

chunks.h: Can I load relations on a write, or count them?
chunks.t: Yes. create, update, upsert and the mass writes take options.relations and return the rows with them loaded, and a create body can write children too. See Relations on writes (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations-on-writes). options.counts adds _count for collections; see Aggregates (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates).

- → Primary keys: including uuid, which affects relation FKs (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/primary-keys)
- → Filtering: the full filter spec including operator reference (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering)

chunks.h: Relations on writes, nested create, attach and detach
chunks.t:
Return created and updated rows with their relations loaded, create has-many and belongs-to children in one transaction, and attach, detach or sync many-to-many links.

create, update, upsert, restore and every mass write take options.relations and return the rows with those relations loaded, using the same batched loaders as a read. Nested create, behind writableRelations, writes children in the same transaction, and attach, detach and sync change many-to-many links with set-based statements.

chunks.p: Relations on writes, nested create, attach and detach
chunks.h: How do I get a created row back with its relations?
chunks.t:
Pass relations (and counts, see Aggregates (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates)) as you would on find:

That is one INSERT plus one query per relation. A mass write loads the relations of every row it wrote in one query per relation too, so massCreate of 10 posts with relations: ['author'] is an INSERT and one SELECT, not ten.

update, upsert, massUpsert, massUpdate, restore and massRestore work the same way. The relation paths are checked against loadableRelations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) before anything is written, so a bad path is a 400 and leaves the table untouched.

chunks.p: Relations on writes, nested create, attach and detach
chunks.h: How do I create a row with its children in one call?
chunks.t:
List the relation in writableRelations, then put it in the body under the relation's name:

The author and both posts are written in one transaction: an INSERT for the author and one multi-row INSERT for the posts, with author_id set for you. If a child fails, the parent is rolled back and the call answers with the child's error (a bad enum value is a 400, a duplicate key a 409).

chunks.p: Relations on writes, nested create, attach and detach
chunks.h: What shapes does a nested body take?
chunks.t:
Relation Body value What happens 
--- --- --- 
has-many an array of objects One multi-row INSERT, with the foreign key set to the new row's key. 
belongs-to an object The parent is inserted first and its key goes on the row (localKey). 
many-to-many an array of ids, objects, or both Objects are inserted into the related table in one statement, then every id is linked through the join table. 

Nested writes are one level deep. Only the related table's own columns are written, never its soft delete column, and its timestamps and the tenant scope (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy) are set when the related table has those columns. Nested create needs RETURNING, so it runs on PostgreSQL; on MySQL it is a 400.

chunks.p: Relations on writes, nested create, attach and detach
chunks.h: What if writableRelations is not set?
chunks.t: Nested writes are off. A relation key in the body is left alone and Drizzle ignores it, which is how 3.4 behaved. With the list set, a relation key that is not in it is a 400, the same way writableColumns (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) treats a column.

chunks.p: Relations on writes, nested create, attach and detach
chunks.h: How do I attach or detach many-to-many rows?
chunks.t: Each method returns the row with that relation loaded (plus anything in options.relations) and runs in one transaction. They are set based whatever the number of ids: one SELECT checks the targets exist, one finds the links already there, and one INSERT adds the rest. Ids already linked are skipped, and duplicates in the list are ignored. The related rows themselves are never changed or deleted.

c.s:
await posts.attach(2, 'tags', [1, 2]);        // link tags 1 and 2
await posts.detach(2, 'tags', [1]);           // unlink tag 1
await posts.detach(2, 'tags');                // unlink every tag
const post = await posts.sync(2, 'tags', [2]); // links are exactly [2] now
post.tags; // [{ id: 2, name: 'tech' }]

chunks.t:

- A target id that does not exist or is soft-deleted: a 400 BulkOperationException with one 404 entry per missing id.
- When the related table has the scope column, a target of another tenant counts as missing.
- The relation is not a many-to-many: 400.
- writableRelations is set and does not list the relation: 400. Unset, attach, detach and sync work on any many-to-many relation.

They raise attach, detach and sync events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events) when global hooks are on.

PostgreSQL SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / SHARE / NO KEY UPDATE on find, findOne, and findAll via SqlOperationOptions.

On PostgreSQL, find, findOne, and findAll accept a row-level lock in their third argument (SqlOperationOptions). The package wraps the generated SELECT with Drizzle's.for(...) clause. On MySQL the lock options are no-ops. The option is silently ignored, and no FOR UPDATE is generated.

Read-modify-write patterns where you need to prevent another transaction from mutating the row between your read and your update:

- Fetching an account balance, then decrementing it.
- Locking a posts row while computing a slug.
- Anything where a stale read would cause a lost-update bug.

If you only need to fetch data and write it later, prefer executeSqlTransaction and call select(...).for('update') directly. Locks are scoped to the transaction and released on commit or rollback.

Two fields on SqlOperationOptions. Both Postgres-only:

Field Type SQL it produces 
--- --- --- 
lock 'update' \ 'share' \ 'none' FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE / (omitted) 
forNoKeyUpdate boolean FOR NO KEY UPDATE 

lock: 'none' is the default. Pass it explicitly to override a service-level default. lock and forNoKeyUpdate are mutually exclusive; forNoKeyUpdate wins if both are set.

FOR NO KEY UPDATE is like FOR UPDATE but does not block other transactions from inserting FK-target rows. Useful when you're locking a parent row but children may legitimately appear (e.g. appending audit-log entries).

Can I lock a row and eager-load a belongs-to relation?. Yes. The lock always names the base table (FOR UPDATE OF <table ), so only the service's own rows are locked and the LEFT JOINed relation is not. Before 3.3.1 the lock covered every table in the query, and Postgres refused it with FOR UPDATE cannot be applied to the nullable side of an outer join.

c.s:
const account = await accounts.find(id, { lock: 'update' });
// SELECT ... FOR UPDATE OF "accounts"

chunks.t: Yes. The lock always names the base table (FOR UPDATE OF <table ), so only the service's own rows are locked and the LEFT JOINed relation is not. // SELECT ... FROM posts LEFT JOIN users ... FOR UPDATE OF "posts"

chunks.t:
- MySQL. The options are accepted but ignored. No FOR UPDATE is added. If you need MySQL locking, drop down to a custom method.
- No assertions under contention. The package's unit tests cover the code path (the option reaches Drizzle's.for(...)); contention behavior is the database's contract, not ours. Verify with a concurrent integration test before relying on it.
- Read methods only. create / update / delete / softDelete / restore have their own transaction model. They don't take a lock option. Use executeSqlTransaction and a find(..., { lock }) inside it if you need to lock across reads and writes.

Enable soft delete with a deleted_at column, restore rows, list the trash with onlyDeleted or withDeleted, and purge rows for good with forceDelete.

Soft delete sets a deleted_at timestamp on a row instead of removing it. Reads (find, findOne, findAll, findByCursor, count) exclude soft-deleted rows unless you pass withDeleted or onlyDeleted; restore(id) clears the column and brings the row back, and forceDelete(id) removes it for good.

Globally (default for all entities). The package looks for a column under the key deleted_at by default. The setting names the key in your Drizzle table object, not the database column name. With a camelCase schema such as deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at'), set column: 'deletedAt'.

A missing column fails at startup. 
Since 3.3.1 the service checks the soft-delete column when it is built. If
the table has no key by that name, startup fails with a message that names
the key to use, for example: softDelete.column is "deleted_at", but the
table has no column under that key. The column "deleted_at" is declared
under the key "deletedAt"; set softDelete.column to "deletedAt".
Before 3.3.1 the same mistake made every read fail with a 500.

Per-entity (different column name or disable for one entity). Per-entity config overrides the global default, and merges with it: { softDelete: { column: 'archivedAt' } } keeps enabled from the project setting. The column is the key in your Drizzle table object; the package uses it in WHERE clauses and in SET / UPDATE statements.

`softDelete(id, options?)` → `Promise<boolean>`. Returns true if the row was found and marked deleted, false if it didn't exist.

`restore(id, options?)` → `Promise<T>`. Throws EntityNotFoundException if the row didn't exist (or didn't have a soft-delete column set). Returns the restored entity on success.

restore is independent of soft-delete state. It will happily
re-restore a row that wasn't soft-deleted (effectively a no-op on
the column). To check whether a row is in the trash, read it with
onlyDeleted: await users.exists(42, { onlyDeleted: true }).

`massSoftDelete(ids, options?)` → `Promise<boolean>`. Same as softDelete for a set of ids: one SELECT to check they exist and one UPDATE... WHERE id IN (...), in a transaction. If any id does not exist or is already in the trash, nothing changes and BulkOperationException lists the ids that failed. massRestore(ids) is the reverse.

chunks.h: How do I list soft-deleted rows?
chunks.t:
Pass onlyDeleted: true for the trash view, or withDeleted: true for live and deleted rows together. Both work on every read: find, findOne, findAll, findByCursor, count, exists and fullTextSearch.

The flags only change the service's own table. Related tables keep hiding their soft-deleted rows, so an eager-loaded parent that is in the trash still comes back as null. onlyDeleted on an entity without soft delete is a 400.

A filter on the column itself, such as { deletedAt: { isNotNull: true } }, still returns nothing without one of the flags, because the default deleted_at IS NULL is ANDed with it.

Over HTTP, parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing) reads?onlyDeleted=true and?withDeleted=true, but only when you opt in with allowTrash: true. Without it they are unknown filter columns, so a client cannot open the trash on a route that is not meant to show it.

chunks.h: How do I purge a soft-deleted row?
chunks.t:
forceDelete(id) hard-deletes the row whether it is in the trash or not, and runs the delete hooks. massForceDelete(ids) does the same for a set of ids in one statement.

delete(id) keeps its meaning: it only sees live rows, so it answers 404 for a row that is already in the trash. The same is true of massDelete. Both delete and forceDelete accept the same options, so delete(id, { withDeleted: true }) is the long way of writing forceDelete(id).

c.s:
await users.forceDelete(42);           // gone, even if it was soft-deleted
await users.massForceDelete([7, 8, 9]); // one DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...)

chunks.t:
The column type should accept null (and the package will set it to null on restore and to new Date() on softDelete). This schema uses the camelCase key deletedAt, so its forFeature config needs softDelete: { column: 'deletedAt' }.

If the column doesn. 
If your table has no soft-delete column, set
defaults: { softDelete: false } (or per-entity
config: { softDelete: { enabled: false } }). Otherwise the service
refuses to start and names the missing key.

The package exposes both softDelete and delete:

Method Behavior 
--- --- 
delete(id, options?) Hard delete, removes the row. Its existence check skips soft-deleted rows, so it answers 404 for a row that is already in the trash. 
forceDelete(id, options?) Hard delete, whether the row is in the trash or not. 
softDelete(id, options?) Sets deleted_at = now(). Reads afterwards exclude it. 
massDelete(ids, options?) Hard delete of live rows, one statement, transactional. 
massForceDelete(ids, options?) Hard delete of live and trashed rows, one statement, transactional. 
massSoftDelete(ids, options?) Soft delete, one statement, transactional. 

Use delete when you really want the row gone (e.g. GDPR right-to-erasure flows). Use softDelete when you want reversibility and audit trails.

The package ships a TestCrudFactory with helpers to construct a working service backed by an in-memory Drizzle instance. The result is a fast unit test that exercises the real base class, findAll, create, hooks, transactions, the lot, without spinning up Postgres or MySQL.

createTestService turns soft delete and timestamps on with the snake_case keys, which createMockTable() has. If you pass a real Drizzle table instead, set softDelete and timestamps to its keys (or turn them off): the service checks them when it is built and throws if one is missing.

chunks.t:
If your service has its own constructor-injected dependencies (event bus, logger, other services), wrap the service in a Nest TestingModule:

Hooks are just methods on the service. The simplest way to verify they fire is to spy on them:

Or override a hook in a test-only subclass:

createMockDb() returns a hand-built stub whose methods are Jest mock functions (select, insert, update, delete, and the chainable from / where / limit / offset / orderBy / returning). It runs no SQL. You decide what a query resolves to by setting the mock's return value, which is what makes these tests fast and deterministic.

Two consequences to plan for:

- It needs a Jest environment. The factory calls the global jest, so it works inside a Jest test file and nowhere else.
- It does not verify your SQL. A stub cannot catch a wrong column name, a bad cast, or a constraint violation. Cover those with an end-to-end test against a real database, the way this project's own apps/api e2e suite does: Playwright drives the app over HTTP while the app runs against PGlite (https://pglite.dev), Postgres compiled to WASM, in-process. That needs no container and no credentials, so there is no excuse for skipping the SQL-level test.

createMockTable() returns a plain object whose keys stand in for columns (id, name, email, created_at, updated_at, deleted_at), and createMockEntity(overrides?) returns a row fixture you can override field by field.

If you want tests that exercise real SQL without a server, point createTestService at your own in-memory Drizzle instance, for example pglite (https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite), instead of the stub. The factory takes any db you hand it.

Package-managed vs schema and DB-managed created_at and updated_at, and why DB-managed is recommended.

The package can automatically stamp created_at and updated_at on every write, or you can let your database manage them. The two approaches are mutually exclusive. Pick one per project.

The package uses the application clock and stamps columns only on writes that go through the package:

- create() sets both created_at and updated_at.
- update(), softDelete() and restore() bump updated_at.
- update() with nothing to change is a 400. It does not bump updated_at on its own.

The settings name the keys in your Drizzle table object, created_at / updated_at by default. A camelCase schema (updatedAt: timestamp('updated_at')) needs them set per entity:

chunks.h: Why does my service fail at startup with a timestamps error?
chunks.t:
Because a configured key is not on the table. Before 3.3.1 the package wrote updated_at into the values, Drizzle ignored the unknown key, and updatedAt silently never moved. The service now checks both keys when it is built and stops with a message that names the key to use. Set the keys as above, or turn timestamps off for that entity with timestamps: undefined (or project wide with defaults: { timestamps: false }).

Application clock, partial coverage. 
Package-managed timestamps use the application server's clock, not the
database's. They also only apply to writes through the package. Raw
SQL, migrations, and other code paths won't set them. For
authoritative, wall-clock-accurate, all-write-path timestamps, use
schema/DB-managed.

For authoritative timestamps (database time, on every write path), define them in your Drizzle schema and leave the package's timestamps disabled:

- defaultNow() lets the database set created_at on insert.
- $onUpdate(() = new Date()) makes Drizzle bump updated_at on every update, including the package's own update().

For updated_at that's authoritative even for raw SQL (e.g. a script that runs UPDATE users SET name =... directly), add a Postgres trigger or a MySQL ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP clause:

c.s:
import { pgTable, serial, varchar, timestamp } from 'drizzle-orm/pg-core';

export const users = pgTable('users', {
  id: serial('id').primaryKey(),
  name: varchar('name', { length: 100 }).notNull(),
  email: varchar('email', { length: 255 }).notNull().unique(),

  createdAt: timestamp('created_at', { withTimezone: true })
    .defaultNow()
    .notNull(),

  updatedAt: timestamp('updated_at', { withTimezone: true })
    .defaultNow()
    .notNull()
    .$onUpdate(() => new Date()),

  deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at', { withTimezone: true }),
});

chunks.t: The package will not touch the timestamp columns. The database owns them.
